findings.headline: The Council has just received the Auditors draft report on value for money
findings.detail: The Legal Implications section notes receipt of the draft report and says it gives a third-party objectivity. The paper does not set out the report's findings.
findings.matters: A draft value-for-money report is an external assessment that other councils and lenders would want to see once its findings are published.
findings.quote: the Council has just received the Auditors draft report focusing on value for money

findings.headline: The enhanced fly-tipping and bulky waste trial is extended to 31 March 2027 at an estimated cost of £298k, funded from a Public Realm underspend
findings.detail: The trial was originally due to end on 31 August 2026. The paper says the funding is available for the current year only, and any continuation would require a further Cabinet report with a sustainable funding source.
findings.matters: A finance director can see an unbudgeted service extension funded from an in-year underspend, rather than from a recurring budget line.
findings.figures: £298k estimated extension cost; 31 March 2027 extended end date; 31 August 2026 original end date
findings.quote: The estimated cost of the extension is £298k.

findings.headline: Central resources include a £3.7m underspend from a reduction in employer pension contributions
findings.detail: The paper says the underspend is partly offset the overall pressure and sits within a central expenses position that also includes a £12.150m inflation provision being released to People and Resilience in Period 7.
findings.matters: A pension contribution underspend is a one-year item in the central budget, so the reader can see how much of the overall position depends on it.
findings.figures: £3.7m underspend from reduced employer pension contribution; £12.150m centrally held inflation provision released in Period 7
findings.quote: Separately, the central resources position includes a £3.7m underspend arising from a reduction in the Council

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation has 72 additional clients in more costly forms than budgeted at end of September
findings.detail: The paper links the increase to delays in new-build developments, high homelessness numbers and hostel void delays, and to slow repairs. It also says extended void turnaround times are limiting the benefit of landlord incentive payments.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation demand is a recurring pressure that a finance director at another council facing the same housing market can compare with their own caseload.
findings.figures: 72 additional clients in more costly temporary accommodation than budgeted
findings.quote: led to an additional 72 clients in more costly forms of TA than budgeted for end of September

findings.headline: The HRA is forecasting a nil variance at Period 6, and no longer needs the £2.4m reserve drawdown assumed in the business plan
findings.detail: The paper says the HRA revenue budget will contribute £4.192m to HRA capital financing if the position holds to year-end. The reduced capital programme for 2026/27 is the stated reason.
findings.matters: A break-even HRA that avoids drawing on reserves is a position a finance director can compare with peer HRAs under similar capital pressure.
findings.figures: nil variance at Period 6; £4.192m contribution to HRA capital financing; £2.4m budgeted reserve drawdown no longer required
findings.quote: The HRA is forecasting a nil variance at Period 6.

findings.headline: The 2026/27 capital programme is forecast to deliver £110.179m against a revised budget of £126.904m, an 86.8% delivery rate
findings.detail: Spend to Period 6 is £38.165m. The paper reports 64 schemes with a potential risk of slippage at Period 6, compared with 42 at Period 3, and says a further reprofiling is likely at Period 9.
findings.matters: Slippage against the revised budget and the rise in schemes flagged as at risk show where capital delivery is running behind plan.
findings.figures: £110.179m forecast outturn; £126.904m revised budget; 86.8% delivery rate; £38.165m spend to Period 6; 64 schemes at risk of slippage, up from 42 at Period 3
findings.quote: representing an anticipated delivery rate of approximately 86.8% of the revised programme

findings.headline: The Strategic Commercial Asset Management Delivery Framework is forecast to break even at Period 6 after a £3.9m drawdown from reserves
findings.detail: The paper reports residential pressures from delayed completions and interest rates of about 4.5%–5% against models assuming below 3%. It also reports the Abbey Road and William Street Quarter rent indexation issue and that hotel income is currently in line with budget.
findings.matters: Breakeven depends on a drawdown from reserves, so the reader can see how much of the framework's cost is being met from reserves rather than from income.
findings.figures: £3.9m drawdown from reserves; £1.5m per annum estimated pressure on Abbey Road and William Street Quarter; interest rates of approximately 4.5%–5% against below 3% modelled
findings.quote: are currently forecast to result in an estimated financial pressure of approximately £1.5m per annum

findings.headline: The commercial asset portfolio costs about £10m a year against about £7m of rental income, an annual pressure of about £3m
findings.detail: The paper says the costs comprise borrowing, management and maintenance. The portfolio has been transferred to Inclusive Growth and is being reviewed as a dedicated workstream through the Change Board.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can compare the net cost of a commercial portfolio against its rental yield, and a lender can see the pressure being moved into a separate review.
findings.figures: £10m annual cost; £7m annual rental income; £3m annual pressure
findings.quote: This represents an annual financial pressure of approximately £3m.

findings.headline: £1,142mm of borrowing linked to the Strategic Commercial Asset Management Delivery Framework is due to be refinanced between December 2026 and March 2027
findings.detail: The paper says PWLB interest rates have spiked significantly because of the Middle East war and inflation concerns. It states that because the refinancing will occur later in the year there is no immediate revenue budget impact at this stage.
findings.matters: A lender can see the scale and timing of refinancing against a higher PWLB rate environment, and the paper's own risk assessment is that the cost will show up after the year-end.
findings.figures: £1,142mm of borrowing; £1.6bn total external borrowing; December 2026 to March 2027 refinancing window
findings.quote: This will predominantly require refinancing in the period December 2026 to March 2027.

findings.headline: Usable reserves of £123.4m were brought forward from 2025/26, with £39m stated as available to balance the 2026/27 budget and beyond
findings.detail: The paper lists a £14.6m General Fund Reserve and a £33.3m Budget Support Reserve. It says the Reserve Policy requires a minimum of £12m in the General Fund reserve, and that reserves are being used to manage emerging pressures.
findings.matters: The paper states that reserves are a temporary funding source, so the remaining balance against the size of the overspend is the figure a finance director or lender will track.
findings.figures: £123.4m usable reserves brought forward; £14.6m General Fund Reserve; £33.3m Budget Support Reserve; £12m minimum General Fund reserve; £39m available; £107.50m closing total reserves
findings.quote: the Council had £123.4m of usable reserves brought forward from 2025/26

findings.headline: An indicative High Needs Stability Grant of £2.234m is expected towards the historic DSG deficit, with the first payment due at the end of November 2026
findings.detail: The Government confirmed approval of the SEND Reform Plan on 2 October 2026, which makes the Council eligible for the grant. The paper says the grant relates only to the deficit accumulated to 31 March 2026 and does not fund new 2026/27 SEND expenditure.
findings.matters: Other councils with historic DSG deficits can compare the grant rate of 90% of the eligible deficit and the approval route through the SEND Reform Plan.
findings.figures: £2.234m indicative allocation; 90% of eligible deficit; £2.549m historic deficit
findings.quote: The indicative allocation is £2.234m, with the first payment expected end of November 2026.

findings.headline: The High Needs Block is forecasting a £12.060m in-year DSG overspend, taking the projected DSG deficit to £14.609m
findings.detail: The paper attributes the overspend to demand for SEND provision, including mainstream top-up funding, post-16 placements, ARP places and Home Tuition. It says the deficit will keep growing unless expenditure is reduced or further government funding is confirmed.
findings.matters: A deficit that continues to grow under the statutory accounting override is a liability whose funding treatment the paper describes as uncertain after 31 March 2028.
findings.figures: £12.060m High Needs Block overspend; £14.609m projected DSG deficit at Period 6; £2.549m DSG deficit brought forward
findings.quote: The current DSG overspend of £12.060m results in a projected net deficit of £14.609m at Period 6.

findings.headline: Savings of £1.9m are recorded as delivered against a £10.5m 2026/27 target at Period 6
findings.detail: The paper reports £7.8m on track and £0.6m off track but expected to be delivered within the year. It also records £0.2m of planned savings as unachievable, and says the relevant services must identify alternative savings.
findings.matters: The split between delivered, on-track, off-track and unachievable savings shows how much of the planned budget reduction is still at risk with about half the year remaining.
findings.figures: £10.5m savings target; £1.9m delivered; £7.8m on track; £0.6m off track; £0.2m unachievable
findings.quote: Savings of £1.9m have been delivered to date

findings.headline: Mitigations of £1.841m have been identified in Adults Care & Support at Period 6, the majority of them one-off
findings.detail: The paper says the Adults forecast reflects a structural budget deficit alongside continued demand and transition activity. It also says the position will continue to be closely monitored and reported to Cabinet.
findings.matters: A finance director can read the split between one-off and recurring mitigation as an indicator of whether next year's budget will carry the same pressure.
findings.figures: £1.841m Period 6 mitigations; £9.7m Adults Care & Support overspend
findings.quote: Mitigations of £1.841m have been identified in Period 6, the majority of which are one-off.

findings.headline: People and Resilience is forecasting a £22.7m overspend, with Children Care & Support at £13m and Adults Care & Support at £9.7m
findings.detail: The paper attributes the Children's position mainly to high placement costs, with 31 children coming into care since April 2026. Adults pressures are attributed to sustained demand and rising care costs, with £1.841m of Period 6 mitigations identified, most of them one-off.
findings.matters: Social care is the largest single driver of the General Fund position, and the paper says the mitigations are mostly one-off, which bears on how recurring the overspend will be.
findings.figures: £22.7m People and Resilience overspend; £13m Children Care & Support overspend; £9.7m Adults Care & Support overspend; £1.841m Period 6 mitigations; 31 children came into care since April 2026
findings.quote: Children Care & Support: Net Position £13m Overspend

findings.headline: The General Fund is forecasting a £20.5m overspend at Period 6 against a £266.3m net budget
findings.detail: Forecast expenditure is £286.8m after reserve movements and mitigating actions. The paper says management actions and spending controls must continue to be rigorously applied, and that further measures will be needed to reduce the forecast overspend.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can compare the size of the overspend against budget, and a lender can see how much of the gap management actions are expected to close before year-end.
findings.figures: £20.5m General Fund overspend; £286.8m forecast expenditure; £266.3m net budget
findings.quote: resulting in a forecast General Fund overspend of £20.5m

findings.headline: The 2026/27 capital forecast is £110,179k against a latest budget of £126,904k, while the SCAMDF Residential forecast of £22,743k exceeds its latest budget of £19,953k.
findings.detail: The table gives revised budget, latest budget, spend to 30 September and forecast by scheme. Total spend to date is £38,165k. Of the schemes shown, HRA New Build has a latest budget of £7,865k against a forecast of £792k, and GF Public Realm has a latest budget of £21,339k against a forecast of £16,955k. The paper ties capital programme review to ongoing budgetary pressures.
findings.matters: Scheme-level variances in both directions, including a forecast above budget on the Framework's residential programme and a large forecast shortfall on HRA New Build, show where slippage and cost pressure are sitting for finance teams tracking their own capital plans.
findings.figures: Grand total revised budget £169,459k; latest budget £126,904k; spend to date £38,165k; forecast £110,179k; SCAMDF Residential latest budget £19,953k, forecast £22,743k; HRA New Build latest budget £7,865k, forecast £792k
findings.quote: This table shows the revised estimates for capital expenditure and

findings.headline: The paper forecasts a £3.9m loss on the Strategic Commercial Asset Management Delivery Framework and a break-even position on the General Fund's investment income.
findings.detail: The recommendations give the forecast investment income outturn for 2026/27. Investments outstanding at 30 September 2026 total £525.5m, of which £428.3m sits in the Strategic Commercial Asset Management Delivery Framework and £97.2m in the General Fund. The paper gives no explanation for the forecast loss.
findings.matters: A forecast loss on a £428.3m investment book is a direct income pressure on the Council's budget, and a lender or peer finance officer will want to know that the Framework is forecasting a loss rather than a return.
findings.figures: £3.9m forecast loss (SCAMDF); break-even (General Fund); investments £525.5m total; SCAMDF £428.3m; General Fund £97.2m; cash deposits £35.6m; loans and equity £489.9m
findings.quote: a break-even position on the General Fund and £3.9m loss on the Strategic Commercial

findings.headline: The 10-year gilt reached 5.18% in mid-May 2026, its highest level since 2008, after ending March at 4.92%.
findings.detail: The paper says gilt yields and PWLB Certainty Rates were volatile over the six months and generally moved higher. The 50-year PWLB Certainty Rate rose from 6.00% on 01/04/2026 to 6.37% on 30/09/2026. MUFG expects Bank Rate to rise to 4% in the near term, with rates falling back over one to three years.
findings.matters: Replacement funding for maturing debt and any future borrowing will be priced off these gilt and PWLB movements, so a finance director at another council or a lender will want the trajectory the paper reports.
findings.figures: 10-year gilt 4.92% end March, 5.18% mid-May high, 5.43% end September; PWLB 50-year 6.00% on 01/04/2026, 6.37% on 30/09/2026, high 6.48%; Bank Rate 3.75% with an anticipated rise to 4%
findings.quote: after ending March at 4.92%, the 10-year Gilt shot up to 5.18% in mid-May, its highest level since 2008

findings.headline: £430.5m (27%) of borrowing falls in the 0 to 1 year period and £444.5m (28%) in the 1 to 5 year period, with an average rate of 3.39%.
findings.detail: The paper's maturity table splits the £1,586.3m portfolio by period. The 0 to 1 year and 1 to 5 year bands together account for 55% of the portfolio. The paper does not comment on refinancing plans for these periods.
findings.matters: A large share of debt in the shortest periods means the Council will need to refinance or replace funding within five years at whatever rates prevail, which matters to peers planning their own refinancing and to lenders assessing that concentration.

findings.headline: Total Council borrowing stands at £1,586.3m, of which £1,142m relates to the Strategic Commercial Asset Management Delivery Framework, £294.3m to the Housing Revenue Account and £150m to the General Fund.
findings.detail: The paper's recommendations set out total council borrowing by fund. Section 5.1 gives the 2026/27 capital financing requirement as £1,997m, which the paper describes as the underlying need to borrow for capital purposes. Section 5.2 says further borrowing is anticipated this financial year if necessary.
findings.matters: A finance director comparing borrowing with the capital financing requirement, and a lender assessing exposure to one Council's commercial framework, both need the split between the Framework and the other funds.
findings.figures: £1,586.3m total borrowing; £1,142m SCAMDF; £294.3m HRA; £150m General Fund; CFR £1,997m
findings.quote: Total Council borrowing of £1,586.3m, of which £1,142m related to the Strategic Commercial Asset Management Delivery Framework

findings.headline: Westrow Drive has no mitigation option and no economic appraisal, because Thames Water has not provided pumping station data needed to establish the baseline risk
findings.detail: The paper identifies 91 properties at internal flood risk at the 1 in 100 annual chance event at Westrow Drive. It says the baseline risk cannot be established with sufficient confidence without the pump data.
findings.matters: A council depending on a partner authority's data for a costed scheme faces a delay that a finance director would need to factor into timing and funding applications.
findings.figures: 91 properties at risk of internal flooding at the 1 in 100 annual chance event; 18 at 1 in 30; 409 at 1 in 1000 (total)
findings.quote: No mitigation scenario has been modelled and no economic appraisal has been completed for Westrow Drive.

findings.headline: No Section 19 flood investigation reports were completed and published in the 2017 to 2023 period, though the process was agreed
findings.detail: The paper says the commitment is strengthened in the new strategy through published thresholds and annual reporting. It also says the Section 19 investigations are carried forward in Annex A, measure 1.2.
findings.matters: Statutory investigation reports not being published is a governance gap that other councils' finance and scrutiny officers would check for in their own flood duties.
findings.figures: zero Section 19 investigation reports completed and published in the 2017 to 2023 period
findings.quote: No Section 19 investigation reports were completed and published during the period, although the process for undertaking them was agreed.

findings.headline: Of 23 actions in the 2017 to 2023 flood strategy, the paper reports 10 delivered, 9 partly delivered, 2 superseded and 1 not delivered
findings.detail: The paper lists one remaining action on reservoir flood risk as in progress. It says the Section 19 commitment and several others are carried forward into the 2026 to 2032 Action Plan.
findings.matters: A finance officer assessing the delivery record of a predecessor strategy can see how many committed actions were completed, which bears on the credibility of the new plan's timescales.
findings.figures: 23 actions in total; 10 delivered; 9 partly delivered; 2 superseded; 1 not delivered; 1 in progress
findings.quote: Of these, 10 were delivered, 9 were partly delivered, 2 were superseded by a different approach and 1 was not delivered.

findings.headline: The Council says it does not know the full cost of addressing surface water flood risk across the Borough, beyond the three appraised schemes
findings.detail: The paper notes that three locations have no costed option, three further priority areas have not been assessed, and the pipeline schemes are costed separately. The restated £1.96 million figure covers only the three appraised schemes.
findings.matters: A finance director can see that the paper's total cost figure is partial, and that the full programme cost is not yet quantified in this Council's own documents.
findings.figures: £1.96 million restated combined cost of three schemes; three further priority areas and Westrow Drive not costed
findings.quote: The true cost of addressing surface water flood risk across the Borough is therefore considerably higher than £1.96 million, and the Council does not currently know what it is.

findings.headline: Benefit to cost ratios on flood damages alone are 2.92 for Heathway Industrial Estate, 1.43 for Rylands Estate and 0.14 for Parsloes Park
findings.detail: The paper reports Parsloes Park as not viable on flood damages alone. It says the Council is considering property flood resilience there instead, unless a wider benefits case is made. These ratios use the 2019 appraisal figures.
findings.matters: A ratio below one means a scheme's avoided damage does not cover its cost, which affects which schemes a council can put forward for national funding ranking.
findings.figures: benefit to cost ratios 2.92 (Heathway Industrial Estate), 1.43 (Rylands Estate), 0.14 (Parsloes Park); present value of benefits £116,184 at Parsloes Park against costs of £808,513
findings.quote: Parsloes Park does not achieve a benefit to cost ratio above one on flood damages alone

findings.headline: Every scheme in the Borough's pipeline falls below the £3 million threshold for 100 per cent government funding under the April 2026 rules
findings.detail: The paper says eligibility is therefore no longer the constraint on delivery. Prioritisation against other authorities' schemes is now the question, and depends on evidence quality and the economic case.
findings.matters: A council whose schemes fall under the threshold may be able to access full government funding, a change that other councils with similar pipelines would also need to assess.
findings.figures: £3 million threshold for 100 per cent government funding; 90 per cent above that threshold
findings.quote: Every scheme in the Borough’s current pipeline falls below the £3 million threshold at which full government funding is available.

findings.headline: The paper says construction inflation has overtaken the 60 per cent optimism bias allowance in the 2019 appraisal, leaving no remaining risk allowance in the published totals
findings.detail: The paper states that the published totals carry no remaining allowance for land purchase, ground conditions, buried services and other excluded items. It advises the Council to expect out-turn costs to exceed the restated figures.
findings.matters: A finance officer relying on an appraisal's contingency to cover price rises should check whether that contingency is still intact, since the paper reports it has been used up by inflation alone.
findings.figures: base construction cost £404,126; restated central estimate approximately £667,000; published total including 60 per cent optimism bias £646,080
findings.quote: construction inflation alone has now overtaken the entire optimism bias

findings.headline: Restating the three appraised flood alleviation schemes at 2026 prices raises their combined central cost from £1.19 million to approximately £1.96 million
findings.detail: The increase is around £770,000 on the central estimate. The paper gives a range of £1,759,000 to £2,104,000 across the two price base assumptions it uses.
findings.matters: Capital cost estimates carried from a 2010 to 2015 price base understate what an out-turn will cost, which affects any finance director relying on older appraisals for budgeting or bids.
findings.figures: £1.19 million to approximately £1.96 million; increase of around £770,000; range £1,759,000 to £2,104,000
findings.quote: On the central estimate the combined cost of the three schemes rises from £1.19 million to approximately £1.96 million

findings.headline: The 2019 appraisal's indicated grant leaves a shortfall of £854,586 across the Parsloes Park and Rylands Estate schemes, under the funding rules in place when they were appraised
findings.detail: The paper says the Council would have had to find this sum under the 2019 funding rules, and that it is a substantial part of why the schemes have not been built. It states that the position is superseded by the April 2026 rules.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can compare this historic gap with the grant position under the new national rules before committing match funding to a similar scheme.
findings.figures: £854,586 shortfall; around £763,000 at Parsloes Park; around £91,000 at Rylands Estate; grant indicated in 2019 £467,735 against a combined cost of £1,188,426
findings.quote: The shortfall the Council would actually have had to find is therefore approximately £854,586

findings.headline: The Flood Mitigation Study reports that three locations previously assumed to be at risk do not present significant risk to property
findings.detail: The Flood Mitigation Study tested the areas of concern from the 2011 Surface Water Management Plan and modelled four Critical Drainage Areas in detail. The report says three locations previously assumed to be at risk do not present significant risk to property. The Council describes this as the principal achievement of the previous strategy's evidence base.
findings.matters: A finding that reduces the assumed number of at-risk locations changes where flood capital is directed, and a reader can compare it with the approach taken in other councils' surface water plans.
findings.figures: 3 locations previously assumed at risk; 4 Critical Drainage Areas modelled in detail
findings.quote: three locations previously assumed to be at risk do not present significant risk to property

findings.headline: Scheme costs in the Strategy are indicative, drawn from feasibility-stage work, and no expenditure is committed by approving the report
findings.detail: The report says approval commits no expenditure and that the Strategy does not authorise works. Scheme costs are indicative and will be confirmed through a business case for each scheme, including whole-life maintenance costs. Where a scheme creates additional expenditure commitments, separate approval will be sought.
findings.matters: Indicative feasibility costs in a policy document are not the same as approved capital budgets, and a reader comparing against another council's flood programme needs that distinction.
findings.figures: None given in the extract provided
findings.quote: Scheme costs quoted in the Strategy are indicative and drawn from feasibility stage work.

findings.headline: Barking Town East outline business case reviewed by the Environment Agency; two further business cases in preparation
findings.detail: The report says the Barking Town East outline business case has been reviewed by the Environment Agency. It says business cases for Mayesbrook Ward Area and Heathway Industrial Estate are in preparation, and that a joint scheme at St Chad's is being developed with the London Borough of Redbridge.
findings.matters: A finance officer can track which flood schemes have reached business-case stage, and which are still at feasibility, before any capital commitment is sought.
findings.figures: 1 outline business case reviewed; 2 business cases in preparation; 1 joint scheme in development
findings.quote: The Barking Town East outline business case has been reviewed by the Environment Agency

findings.headline: National flood and coastal erosion funding changed in April 2026 to an outcome-based allocation, weighted towards deprivation
findings.detail: The report says funding is now allocated on the outcomes a scheme delivers per pound of government investment, with weight given to deprivation. It presents the evidence base and a clear pipeline as the means of improving the Council's position in that process. The Strategy's funding routes are set out in Section 10 of the draft.
findings.matters: A change to how central flood money is allocated affects every council competing for it, and the report ties the Council's access to external funds to its evidence base.
findings.figures: April 2026 (date of the funding change)
findings.quote: National funding changed in April 2026 and is now allocated on the basis of the outcomes a scheme delivers for each pound of government investment, with weight given to deprivation.

findings.headline: The Council's current flood risk strategy covered 2017 to 2023 and requires replacement
findings.detail: The Flood and Water Management Act 2010 requires the Council to develop, maintain, apply and monitor a local flood risk strategy. The report says bringing forward the 2026 to 2032 draft returns the Council to full compliance. The risk table records that adoption is to stay within the current municipal year.
findings.matters: A statutory plan has lapsed, and a reader can check whether the replacement is adopted on the timetable the report sets out.
findings.figures: 2017 to 2023 (expired strategy period); 2026 to 2032 (draft period)
findings.quote: The Council’s current Strategy covered the period 2017 to 2023 and requires replacement.

findings.headline: The 2017 to 2023 flood strategy's 23 actions: 10 delivered, 9 partly delivered, 2 superseded, 1 not delivered
findings.detail: The report gives the outcome of each action in the expired strategy. It names one shortfall: no Section 19 investigation reports were completed and published, although the process for them was agreed. The asset register and risk-based maintenance were only partly completed, and community flood groups were not established to the extent intended. The remaining reservoir action is in progress.
findings.matters: A finance director at this or another council can compare the delivery rate of a flood programme against the stated plan, and see which commitments carried forward into the new Action Plan.
findings.figures: 23 actions; 10 delivered; 9 partly delivered; 2 superseded by a different approach; 1 not delivered
findings.quote: The 2017 to 2023 Strategy contained 23 actions. Ten were delivered, nine were partly delivered, two were superseded by a different approach and one was not delivered.

findings.headline: The Council has been without a current adopted local flood risk strategy since 2023, and the draft 2026 to 2032 Strategy is being put forward for public consultation.
findings.detail: The screening records that the duty to prepare, consult on and publish the Strategy is statutory. Approving the draft for consultation is described as addressing the gap, and delegated authority to adopt the final Strategy is sought after consultation.
findings.matters: A statutory strategy that has lapsed is an open compliance item, and councils elsewhere may be in the same position; the consultation and adoption steps are the route to closing it.
findings.quote: the Council has been without a current adopted Strategy since 2023

findings.headline: National flood investment arrangements introduced in April 2026 direct at least 20 per cent of national investment to the most deprived fifth of communities.
findings.detail: The screening says the Strategy's pipeline is designed around these national funding arrangements, and that the change improves the Council's ability to secure investment for the communities most exposed to flooding. The paper also states that the Strategy commits no new expenditure.
findings.matters: A change in how national flood investment is allocated affects where grant funding can be sought, and finance officers at other councils will want to know how the April 2026 rules are being applied locally.
findings.figures: at least 20 per cent of national investment to the most deprived fifth; at least 40 per cent to the two most deprived fifths
findings.quote: it sets out a pipeline designed around the national funding arrangements introduced in April 2026, under which at least 20 per cent of national investment is directed to the most deprived fifth of communities

findings.headline: Cabinet would authorise disposal costs up to 10% of gross receipts across the programme, with fees above asset values acknowledged in the report.
findings.detail: The report accepts that some fees exceed the value of the asset and justifies them as removing liability on poor-performing sites. It says a discounted fee structure is expected from the size of the instruction, and that Savills and Auction House London have been engaged.
findings.matters: A cost ceiling tied to gross receipts sets a limit on how much of each sale is lost to fees, a benchmark other councils can compare with their own disposal costs.
findings.figures: Maximum cost level of 10% of gross receipts; minimum net receipt target of 90%
findings.quote: Cabinet will authorise a maximum cost level of 10% of gross receipts across the programme.

findings.headline: The report says disposing of income-producing assets will reduce council revenue, with no figure given for the income lost.
findings.detail: The report states the loss will be outweighed by capital receipts and that the council will retain a healthy commercial portfolio. It screens assets for disposal partly on rents below £10,000 per annum, as these are unlikely to cover management costs.
findings.matters: Income forgone from disposals is a recurring cost to the revenue budget that finance directors weigh against one-off receipts, and an unquantified loss makes that trade-off hard to assess.
findings.figures: Rent screening threshold of under £10,000 per annum; no figure given for lost revenue
findings.quote: Disposing of income producing assets will theoretically reduce the overall revenue collected by the Council.

findings.headline: The financial implications section describes the net expected return as £5.8m, while the receipt table sets the net target at £5,247,900.
findings.detail: Section 6.1 states the net expected return after disposal costs and fees is £5.8m, based on the reserve guide price. Section 2.9 gives an indicative gross receipt of £5,831,000 and a 90% net target of £5,247,900, so the two net figures in the paper differ.
findings.matters: A reader relying on the headline figure could overstate the net cash from the programme by roughly £0.6m if the table's 90% target is the measure that applies.
findings.figures: £5.8m net expected return (section 6.1); £5,831,000 indicative receipt and £5,247,900 at 90% net (section 2.9)
findings.quote: The Net expected return after disposal costs / fees is £5.8m based on the Reserve Guide price

findings.headline: Officers will target a net receipt after costs of 90%, which the report puts at £5,247,900 across both tranches against an indicative £5,831,000.
findings.detail: The target receipt summary gives Tranche 1 at £3,198,000 indicative (£2,878,200 at 90% net) and Tranche 2 at £2,633,000 indicative (£2,369,700 at 90% net). Where 90% is not achievable, officers must justify disposal costs through a cost/benefit analysis.
findings.matters: The gap between gross indicative receipts and net targets sets the cash the council can expect after sale costs, which matters when capital receipts are earmarked for other projects.
findings.figures: Tranche 1 £3,198,000 indicative, £2,878,200 at 90% net; Tranche 2 £2,633,000 indicative, £2,369,700 at 90% net; project total £5,831,000 indicative, £5,247,900 at 90% net
findings.quote: The officers will target a minimum net receipt after costs of 90%.

findings.headline: Be First has reviewed 449 commercial assets and shortlisted 2 tranches of freehold sites for disposal, with Tranche 1 targeted before 31 March 2027 and an indicative £5.8m receipt.
findings.detail: The report proposes disposing of 19 Tranche 1 properties by 31 March 2027 and 23 Tranche 2 properties in subsequent financial years, subject to asset management initiatives. Estimated sale prices come from a desktop appraisal and will be refined by site visits.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can compare the scale of a disposal programme, its timetable and the basis of its receipt estimate against their own asset sales plans.
findings.figures: 449 assets; £5.8m indicative receipt; Tranche 1 target before 31 March 2027
findings.quote: Be First reviewed the full commercial portfolio of 449 assets to determine which assets may be suitable for disposal.

findings.headline: The draft Strategy will state that funding is not secured for every scheme in its prioritised pipeline.
findings.detail: The risks section says the summary and drop-in briefing will state plainly that the Strategy sets a framework and a prioritised pipeline, and that funding is not secured for every scheme. It refers readers to Section 10 of the Strategy for the funding position.
findings.matters: Flood schemes in a council pipeline without secured funding are a capital exposure that finance officers at other councils will also be tracking.
findings.quote: funding is not secured for every scheme

findings.headline: The consultation will be delivered within existing resources, with no separate budget set out in the paper.
findings.detail: Section 11 of the paper states the consultation is to be delivered within existing resources. It names Flood Risk Management, Communications and Consultation, Legal, and Strategy and Equalities as the teams carrying the work.
findings.matters: A finance officer would note that the consultation, a statutory step, is being resourced from existing budgets rather than a new allocation.
findings.quote: The consultation is to be delivered within existing resources.

findings.headline: Barking and Dagenham has had no current adopted local flood risk strategy since the 2017 to 2023 Strategy expired, and the draft 2026 to 2032 Strategy goes to Cabinet on 10 November 2026.
findings.detail: The paper states the council has been without a current adopted strategy since the earlier one expired. It sets a timetable with consultation closing on 12 February 2027 and submission for adoption under delegated authority by 31 March 2027.
findings.matters: A finance director at this or another council would want to know when the flood risk framework that sets the scheme pipeline will be in force, and this paper gives a dated target for that.
findings.figures: 2017 to 2023 Strategy; 2026 to 2032 Strategy; consultation closes 12 February 2027; adoption submission by 31 March 2027
findings.quote: The Council has been without a current adopted local strategy since the 2017 to 2023 Strategy expired.

findings.headline: Hermes Infrastructure has delivered negative returns while benchmarks are positive, underperforming by 7.70% over 12 months
findings.detail: Infrastructure is allocated 3.77% of the fund. Hermes Infrastructure returned -1.80% over the 12 months to June against a 5.90% benchmark (underperformance of 7.70%), and -1.80% in Q2 against 1.44% benchmark (underperformance of 3.25%).
findings.matters: A fund manager delivering negative real returns when the benchmark is positive creates a sustained drag on overall returns and suggests either poor management or an unsuitable asset class allocation
findings.figures: -1.80% (12m and Q2) vs 5.90% and 1.44% benchmarks respectively; 3.77% allocation

findings.headline: Kempen Capital Management, a major fund manager, significantly underperformed in Q2, returning only 3.92% against a benchmark of 13.03%
findings.detail: Kempen is allocated 16.08% of the fund (the second-largest allocation). Its Q2 return of 3.92% against a 13.03% benchmark represents a 9.10% underperformance, though its 12-month performance is better at 21.18% vs 25.28% benchmark (-4.10%).
findings.matters: A 9.10% Q2 shortfall on a 16% fund allocation represents a material drag on returns and raises questions about manager performance and suitability

findings.headline: The pension fund has underperformed its investment benchmark across all time periods
findings.detail: In the quarter to June, the fund returned 7.28% against a benchmark of 8.64% (shortfall of 1.36%). Over 12 months it returned 14.48% against 16.60% (shortfall of 2.12%). Over three years it returned 11.35% against 12.82% (shortfall of 1.47%). This persistent underperformance is material.
findings.matters: Consistent underperformance against the benchmarks that underpin the actuarial valuation increases the risk that employer contribution rates will need to rise at the next triennial revaluation, creating pressure on the council's revenue budget
findings.quote: During the quarter the Fund returned 7.28% against the benchmark 8.64%, resulting in an underperformance of negative return of 1.36%

findings.headline: The Strategic Commercial Asset Management Delivery Framework (£2bn capital investment, 60 schemes) is no longer financially viable under current interest rates and may require business case revision
findings.detail: The council is implementing a major regeneration and housing programme involving £2bn of capital investment across 60 schemes, generating 2,000 residential units already built/in development and providing anticipated commercial income to support the budget. However, rising PWLB borrowing costs mean that new schemes no longer generate sufficient returns to cover long-term financing costs. The paper notes that while no changes are proposed to the currently-approved business case assumptions yet, officers will continue to monitor interest rates and may need to revise assumptions around tenure and grant.
findings.matters: This commercial framework is material to the council's financial plan and has been approved on specific return assumptions. If viability fails or the business case is revised downwards, this represents a significant hit to anticipated income and a material unplanned source of additional borrowing. It also demonstrates the council's exposure to interest rate risk on long-dated borrowing.
findings.figures: £2bn capital investment, 60 schemes, 2,000 residential units built and 1,500 in development, £2.8m additional funding requirement for asset management function
findings.quote: Given the significant rise in borrowing costs relative to the Council's historic Public Works Loan Board (PWLB) average, new schemes no longer generate sufficient returns to offset financing costs without revised assumptions around tenure and grant.

findings.headline: General Fund reserves have depleted to critical levels with only £2.6m available for emergencies beyond the minimum policy requirement
findings.detail: Usable reserves fell from £123.4m to £112.93m in one year. Of this, the General Fund reserve is £14.59m, and council policy requires a minimum of £12m. This leaves only £2.6m available for other purposes. Additionally, the council now acknowledges that the £12m minimum (representing less than 5% of net budget) is insufficient given current financial risks and uncertainty.
findings.matters: Thin reserves provide minimal buffer for unexpected pressures or failed savings plans. The council's own S151 officer has flagged that reserve levels are no longer adequate for the scale of risks facing the organisation. This increases vulnerability to further shocks and could force emergency service restrictions or debt default if pressures materialise.
findings.figures: £123.37m → £112.93m reserves, £14.59m General Fund, £12m minimum required, £2.6m available surplus, <5% of net budget
findings.quote: The Council's approved Reserve Policy requires a minimum of £12m to be maintained in the General Fund reserve. Therefore, there is only £2.6m that could be used for other purposes. The current minimum reserve balance of £12m now represents less than 5% of the Council's net budget, which is considered insufficient given the scale of the financial risks facing the organisation.

findings.headline: Budget gap has more than quadrupled from £6.2m (February 2026) to £27.9m (September 2026) for 2027/28, with cumulative gap of £58m over two years
findings.detail: The March 2026 position showed the council could forecast only a £6.2m gap. By September, this has increased to £27.9m for 2027/28 alone, and approximately £58m cumulatively over 2027/28 to 2028/29. The primary drivers are £22.1m in demand pressures from adult social care, children's social care and housing, combined with an in-year 2026/27 overspend crystallising as a recurring baseline pressure. These are structural pressures expected to persist.
findings.matters: A four-fold increase in the budget gap in six months indicates rapidly deteriorating financial position. The council must now find £27.9m in savings annually to balance the budget, and the gap persists due to structural demand that is expected to continue outpacing funding. This directly affects the council's ability to service debt and maintain services.
findings.figures: £27.9m (2027/28 gap), £58m (cumulative 2027/28-2028/29), £22.1m (demand pressures), £6.2m (previous forecast)
findings.quote: The projected budget gap for 2027/28 has increased to £27.9m. The estimated budget gap over the revised MTFS period of 2027/28 to 2028/29 is approximately £58m.

findings.headline: Council must pause Council Tax recovery action and potentially refund enforcement costs
findings.detail: Counsel advises pausing enforcement against the affected resident cohort, avoiding liability orders where arrears arose from the unlawful CTS calculation, and considering refunds of enforcement or recovery costs already incurred. This applies to 1543 affected cases over three years and reduces the council's Council Tax collection income.
findings.matters: This removes collection action against affected cases and creates potential cash outflows for refunding enforcement costs, reducing net Council Tax income.
findings.figures: 1543 cases to be affected across three years
findings.quote: On recovery action, counsel advises that the Council should pause enforcement against the affected cohort, avoid seeking liability orders where the arrears arise from the flaw, and consider refunding enforcement or recovery costs where these have already been incurred.

findings.headline: Correcting the unlawful CTS scheme will cost approximately £439,000 over three years
findings.detail: Modelling estimates a cost pressure of c£439k to correct CTS awards across 2024/25-2026/27 by disregarding the transitional protection element, covering 1014 live claims and 79 no-longer-live cases. The cost will be delivered through Discretionary Council Tax Relief. The projection is an estimate likely subject to change, with potential for further costs as additional affected claims may be identified.
findings.matters: This is a material unplanned cost liability that reduces net income available and may require reserve depletion or service reductions to accommodate.
findings.quote: This projection estimates a cost pressure to restore the level of CTS excluding the TP element of c£439k.

findings.headline: Council Tax Support schemes for 2024/25, 2025/26 and 2026/27 treat Universal Credit transitional protection as income
findings.detail: Counsel has advised that the council's CTS schemes for 2024/25, 2025/26, and 2026/27 are legally vulnerable because they treat Universal Credit transitional protection as income, creating an unlawful discriminatory effect. Following Three Rivers District Council's February 2026 High Court judgment reaching the same finding, counsel advises the position is not defensible and appears discriminatory. The 2026/27 scheme will require change by full Council resolution, and 2027/28 must be compliant.
findings.matters: A lender must assess legal and reputational risk. Three Rivers District Council's similar position led to conceding the claim, refunding affected residents, and paying damages and legal costs.
findings.figures: Three financial years affected (2024/25-2026/27); 1014 live CTS claims identified
findings.quote: Counsel's advice is that the current and recent Council Tax Reduction Schemes are legally vulnerable because they treat Universal Credit transitional protection as income, creating an unlawful discriminatory effect for some residents.

findings.headline: Working-age Council Tax Support claimants required to pay minimum 37% of council tax bill
findings.detail: The CTS scheme provides a maximum discount of 63% for working-age residents, meaning all must pay at least 37% of their bill. The council's risk register identifies that low household financial resilience among CTS recipients creates risk of 'increased arrears, higher recovery and enforcement costs, and potential reputational risk if vulnerable residents are unable to meet their Council Tax payments.' Reducing support further would 'negatively impact collection rates and increase arrears.'
findings.matters: A high proportion of the council's most economically fragile residents cannot fully afford their bills, creating collection volatility and revenue uncertainty
findings.figures: 16,279 CTS claimants in 2026/27 (11,881 working-age, 4,398 pension-age); 37% minimum payment required from working-age households
findings.quote: It would increase Council Tax liability for low-income households, negatively impact collection rates and increase arrears, making it even more difficult to collect Council Tax from the borough's most financially vulnerable residents

findings.headline: Discretionary hardship support demand is rising, with welfare reforms expected to increase pressure further
findings.detail: The Discretionary Council Tax Relief fund received 1,150 individual awards worth £480k in 2025/26. Removal of the Two-Child Cap in Universal Credit from April 2026 is expected to significantly increase demand. The council maintains a minimum £500k fund but caps its General Fund contribution at £500k, relying on external funding from the Greater London Authority to meet demand.
findings.matters: Rising demand for emergency support from vulnerable residents signals increasing financial stress in the borough and suggests underlying affordability challenges are worsening
findings.figures: 1,150 awards in 2025/26 at £480k cost; 2027/28 minimum fund £500k; council contribution capped at £500k
findings.quote: Demand for the DCTR scheme remains high, with more than 1,150 individual awards made in 2025/26 at a total cost of £480k. Further welfare reforms, including the removal of the Two-Child Cap in UC from April 2026, together with ongoing cost-of-living pressures and existing levels of deprivation in the borough, are likely to increase demand for the DCTR scheme

findings.headline: A £572k backdated liability was set aside in the 2025/26 accounts to correct unlawful overpayments
findings.detail: The council treats TP as income since 2024/25. An estimated 836 CTS claims were affected, resulting in unlawful reductions in support. The council is correcting this by using the Discretionary Council Tax Relief scheme to refund affected residents from 2024/25 through 2026/27. A provision was made in the 2025/26 accounts to fund this liability.
findings.matters: While the provision limits immediate impact, it indicates the council was managing contingent liabilities without initially budgeting for the underlying regulatory risk
findings.figures: £572k maximum liability; approximately 836 claims affected; provision established in 2025/26 accounts
findings.quote: A provision was established within the 2025/26 accounts to meet this potential liability and to mitigate any pressure relating to the backdated elements of the proposed corrective action

findings.headline: The council faces legal challenge risk if it does not amend the scheme
findings.detail: The current 2026/27 scheme treats Transitional Protection as income. Retaining this treatment exposes the council to judicial review, as the Three Rivers judgment found this approach 'discriminatory and unlawful.' The council's independent legal counsel has advised that the scheme must be revised to disregard TP as income.
findings.matters: Continued legal exposure creates downside risk to council finances through potential retrospective liability and loss of cases
findings.figures: One High Court judgment (Three Rivers District Council); 861 applicants with TP element in current scheme
findings.quote: If the Council retains the current approach, it could be exposed to legal challenge

findings.headline: Total CTS scheme cost is rising by £997k to £16.3m in 2027/28, increasing the council's budget gap
findings.detail: CTS expenditure will increase from £15.3m in 2026/27 to £16.3m in 2027/28, a 6.5% rise. The increase reflects assumed 4.99% Council Tax growth and the cost of disregarding the TP element. The council acknowledges this cost 'will increase the Council's budget gap if not reflected in the MTFS and budget setting process' and 'will form part of the overall savings requirement needed to maintain a balanced budget.'
findings.matters: Mandatory spending on CTS reduces the discretionary budget available for other council services and increases structural imbalance
findings.figures: £997k increase (+£1.0m noted in text); 2027/28 total £16.309m; 2026/27 total £15.312m
findings.quote: The current CTS scheme is forecast to cost approximately £15.3m in 2026/27, increasing to £16.3m in 2027/28 under the recommended Option 1. This represents an estimated increase of £1.0m

findings.headline: A High Court judgment mandates a £150k annual unbudgeted cost to the council
findings.detail: The Three Rivers District Council judgment found that treating Universal Credit Transitional Protection as income in CTS schemes is unlawful. Barking and Dagenham must now disregard this element for 2027/28 onwards. There is 'currently no specific provision within the MTFS for the additional cost of disregarding the UC TP element, estimated at approximately £0.15m per annum.' This is a recurring pressure that must be accommodated in future budget plans.
findings.matters: Recurring unbudgeted costs reduce financial flexibility and increase the council's budget gap, requiring offsetting savings elsewhere
findings.figures: £150k per annum; approximately 861 affected applicants in current caseload
findings.quote: there is currently no specific provision within the MTFS for the additional cost of disregarding the UC TP element, estimated at approximately £0.15m per annum. This is a recurring pressure arising from the High Court judgment

findings.headline: HRA £10.7m revenue underspend in 2024/25 not identified until final outturn; £4.3m underspend forecast 2025/26
findings.detail: The HRA had a £10.7m revenue underspend in 2024/25, but the magnitude was not identified until the final outturn position was confirmed. This represents a failure of in-year financial monitoring. The 2025/26 budget was set without reflecting the continued impact of this underspend and had to be adjusted recently. A further £4.3m underspend is forecast for 2025/26.
findings.matters: If underspends of this magnitude are missed during the year, so could overspends. This indicates weak in-year monitoring across the Council. The auditor flagged this as needing close monitoring going forward.
findings.figures: £10.7m HRA underspend in 2024/25 (not caught until final outturn); £4.3m forecast underspend 2025/26
findings.quote: The magnitude of the underspend in 2024/25 was not identified until the final outturn position was confirmed. A knock-on impact from this is that when setting the 2025/26 budget in February 2025 the Council did not reflect the continued impact of the 2024/25 underspend.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care represents 70% of budget and remains high-risk despite improved outturn
findings.detail: ASC accounts for 70% of the Council's revenue budget and remains a key area of concern. While outturn improved in 2024/25, external consultant iMPOWER concluded that meaningful change can only be achieved through further investment, not savings. Whether the 2025/26 budget assumptions and growth predictions are realistic remains uncertain. ASC has previously driven major budget variances.
findings.matters: ASC is the largest budget area. If costs spiral due to increased demand or complexity, it could derail the entire financial plan. The auditor is flagging that the improvement may be fragile.
findings.figures: ASC is 70% of council's revenue budget; positive variance in 2024/25; but iMPOWER assessment suggests need for investment, not savings
findings.quote: ASC is still a key area of focus given it accounts for 70% of the Council's revenue budget...The key conclusion by iMPOWER was that meaningful change can only be achieved through further investment. It remains to be seen if the measures and the growth predictions in the 2025/26 budget are reasonable.

findings.headline: Finance team capacity and capability constraints; Chief Accountant departure delayed accounts to mid-July 2025
findings.detail: The Council has insufficient capacity and capability in the finance team to prepare accounts on time. The Chief Accountant left in June 2025, which extended the handover process and delayed accounts production. The team has knowledge gaps, particularly on IFRS16. The Council has been unable to produce complete group accounts for the past two years, and the previous auditor identified errors in group accounts back to 2020/21. A new finance team structure is being implemented from September 2025.
findings.matters: If the finance team cannot produce timely and accurate accounts, how can the Council manage complex financial decisions, subsidiaries, and capital? This is foundational to financial control.
findings.figures: Accounts published mid-July 2025 (after 30 June deadline); Chief Accountant left June 2025; only 50% of audit samples now being provided; new structure implementation September 2025
findings.quote: There are evident resource constraints in the financial accounts team and knowledge gaps, particularly regarding International Finance Reporting Standard IFRS16...The Council has been unable to produce a complete set of group accounts for the past two years.

findings.headline: DSG High Needs Block in emerging deficit; forecast £6.6m overspend will push reserves to -£6m
findings.detail: The High Needs Block of the Dedicated Schools Grant overspent by £6m in 2024/25 and a further £6.6m overspend is forecast for 2025/26. This will move the DSG reserves from an opening £7.75m balance into a £6m deficit. Pressures are from increased SEND provision, out-of-borough placements, and post-16 support. A High Needs Working Group has been tasked to identify mitigating measures, but the auditor flags the need for urgent action.
findings.matters: DSG is a statutory function. A reserves deficit means the Council will have no buffer for further demand shocks. Mitigating actions must be monitored and if insufficient, further urgent action will be needed.
findings.figures: £7.75m opening DSG reserves; £6m overspend in 2024/25; £6.6m forecast overspend 2025/26; resulting £6m deficit
findings.quote: The DSG had a reserves balance of £7.750m at the beginning of 2024/25. However, the High Needs block of the DSG has reported an overspend of over £6m for 2024/25 and a further overspend of £6.6m is currently forecast for 2025/26 which would move the DSG reserves balance into a deficit of £6m.

findings.headline: Council identified as non-compliant with Procurement Act 2023; no Procurement Strategy
findings.detail: The Council has no Procurement Strategy and is non-compliant with several areas of the Procurement Act 2023. The Contracts Register is incomplete and deficient. Multiple waivers have been required (e.g., Street Lighting contract, worth £55m over 5 years, required waivers in both May 2024 and March 2025 due to staffing issues). No corporate oversight of key contract risks or performance. This is a new significant weakness.
findings.matters: Legal non-compliance creates regulatory risk. Lack of procurement strategy prevents the Council from achieving the efficiencies and transformation it needs. Poor contract management and visibility increases spending risk.
findings.figures: Street Lighting contract worth £55m over 5 years needed waivers; one care home spending £20k per quarter on meat that had never been procured (brought down after review)
findings.quote: The Council has identified that it is currently non-compliant in a number of areas relating to the Procurement Act 2023 which came into force with effect from February 2025. The Council currently has no Procurement Strategy.

findings.headline: BDTP £5.9m loan extended twice to March 2026; Barking Riverside £5.5m loan extended to 2034; LEUK ~£29m investment unlikely to be recovered on sale
findings.detail: BDTP's £5.9m loan was extended from July 2024 to March 2025, then again to March 2026 because BDTP was not in a financial position to repay. Barking Riverside's £5.5m loan was extended 9 years to 2034. LEUK was purchased for approximately £29m; the Council acknowledges any sale is unlikely to recover that investment and the company is not returning profit. KPIs and performance monitoring have not been agreed with any of the companies.
findings.matters: These loans tie up Council capital and create financial risk if the companies do not improve. The LEUK investment in particular appears impaired. Lenders need assurance that the Council's exposure to these subsidiaries is manageable.
findings.figures: £5.9m BDTP loan extended twice; £5.5m Barking Riverside loan extended 9 years; ~£29m LEUK investment at risk
findings.quote: In September 2024 Cabinet agreed the extension of the loan of £5.9m to Barking and Dagenham Trading Partnerships Ltd (BDTP), from 31 July 2024 to 31 March 2025...In April 2025 this loan was extended again until 31 March 2026 as BDPT were not in a financial position to repay it.

findings.headline: Investment and Acquisitions Strategy generating £8m losses; no Strategic Asset Management Plan
findings.detail: The IAS outturn for 2024/25 was an adverse variance of £8m, requiring use of reserves to balance the budget. A further £2.6m overspend is forecast for 2025/26. The Council still has no Strategic Asset Management Plan or sustainable IAS strategy. An asset review found lack of data, uncoordinated approach, IAS not achieving targets, and no wider regeneration benefits. This is a new significant weakness.
findings.matters: The IAS is generating recurring losses that drain reserves at a time when the Council is trying to rebuild them. Without a proper asset management plan, the Council cannot control capital spending or deliver regeneration benefits.
findings.figures: £8m adverse variance in 2024/25; £2.6m overspend forecast for 2025/26; lost regeneration benefits not quantified
findings.quote: The IAS outturn for 2024/25 was an adverse variance of £8m requiring the use of reserves of that amount to achieve a balanced budget. A further overspend on the IAS of £2.6m is currently forecast for 2025/26 which will require further use of the IAS reserve.

findings.headline: Transformation programme remains behind schedule with no agreed funding
findings.detail: The Council's transformation programme, which is critical to addressing medium-term funding gaps, has no agreed programme plan. No funding has been secured, and a fully funded plan is unlikely to be in place until 2026/27. The programme requires additional short-term investment, which has not been approved. This is a retained significant weakness from the prior year.
findings.matters: Without a credible transformation plan and funding, the Council cannot close the £12m forecast deficit in 2026/27 or rebuild depleted reserves. This directly threatens medium-term financial sustainability.
findings.figures: MTFS forecast deficit of £12m in 2026/27 rising to £12.7m in 2027/28; £3.5m and £0.18m savings identified but no funded plan to achieve them; transformation programme behind schedule
findings.quote: there is no agreed programme plan. The transformation programme will require additional investment in the short-term but no funding has yet been agreed, and a fully funded plan is unlikely to be in place until 2026/27. The transformation programme is therefore behind schedule.

findings.headline: Auditor plans to issue a disclaimed opinion on the financial statements
findings.detail: The auditor will issue a disclaimed audit opinion on 18 February 2026, not a clean opinion. The Council failed to provide draft accounts by the 30 June 2025 statutory deadline and did not provide supporting working papers until September 2025. The finance team lacks capacity and knowledge gaps on IFRS16. This is a retained significant weakness from the prior year.
findings.matters: A disclaimed opinion means the auditor could not obtain sufficient assurance over the financial statements. Lenders and the s151 officer cannot rely on the numbers as presented; the actual position may be materially different.
findings.figures: Draft accounts published mid-July 2025 (after 30 June deadline); working papers only from September 2025; 50% of audit sample requests now being provided
findings.quote: We plan to issue a disclaimed audit opinion following the Audit and Risk Committee on 18 February 2026...we were hoping to have gained more assurance over the 2024/25 in year transactions and 2024/25 closing balances than we have been able to.

findings.headline: Parks and leisure delivery slowed by contractor insolvencies and DBS compliance issues
findings.detail: The Parks Commissioning programme underspent by £1.496m (68% of budget). The narrative attributes this to: 'Delivery across the parks programme is influenced by weather conditions, site access and contractor availability. A number of contractor insolvencies and DBS requirements for site-based works have also impacted progress.' This indicates market supply-side risks affecting delivery capacity.
findings.matters: Contractor insolvencies in the local supply chain signal economic stress among small capital contractors. This may presage wider delivery issues across the capital programme if the local market is weakening.
findings.figures: Parks Commissioning budget £2,194k, outturn £698k, underspend £1,496k (68%)
findings.quote: A number of contractor insolvencies and DBS requirements for site-based works have also impacted progress. Schemes continue to be closely monitored by the programme manager

findings.headline: ERP Phase 2 project in active vendor negotiation and challenge on application upgrade options
findings.detail: The ERP Phase 2 project spent only £22k of £125k budget and is currently in dispute with its vendor. The narrative states: 'Currently negotiating with the vendor and in a challenge with vendor on options of upgrading the application.' This suggests either cost overrun or scope disputes that are unresolved.
findings.matters: A central finance system upgrade in dispute with the vendor is a governance and operational risk, and may indicate cost pressures or delays ahead on a critical system.
findings.figures: £125.45k budget, £22k outturn, £103k variance
findings.quote: Currently negotiating with the vendor and in a challenge with vendor on options of upgrading the application.

findings.headline: IAS residential and commercial portfolios with multiple major schemes awaiting transfer or transferred
findings.detail: The narrative for IAS (Investment and Asset Strategy) portfolios states that 'a number of major schemes are either transferred or awaiting transfer' with a full operational and delivery update expected at Q1 ACB meeting. This is vague language for portfolio projects at risk, including Sebastian Court (£1.271m), Gascoigne East Phase 2 (£1.042m), and others.
findings.matters: Lenders to IAS portfolios would want clarity on what 'transferred or awaiting transfer' means. This language suggests schemes may be shelved, sold, or fundamentally delayed. These are typically commercial/residential schemes expected to generate revenue.
findings.figures: IAS Residential outturn £118.476m budget £113.893m initial budget; major schemes showing zero carry forward
findings.quote: Within the residential portfolios a number of major schemes are either transferred or awaiting transfer. A full operational and delivery update from managing officers is expected to be presented at the Q1 ACB meeting

findings.headline: Disabled Facilities Grant demand drew forward future-year funding, depleting 2026/27 budget
findings.detail: The DFG programme spent £897k in 2025/26 from a £2.097m budget, but the narrative states: 'Acceleration in 25/26 required partial use of the 26/27 funding.' The council has now received only a £2.3m allocation for 2027/28, which the project manager considers sufficient to meet demand going forward. This indicates demand exceeded available current-year funding.
findings.matters: This shows demand pressures on social care-related capital outstripping budget allocation, forcing the council to draw from future years. It indicates either increasing need or underfunding of a statutory demand.
findings.figures: 2025/26 outturn £897k of £2,097k budget; 2027/28 allocation £2.3m
findings.quote: Acceleration in 25/26 required partial use of the 26/27 funding. The Authority has now received confirmation of the 27/28 DFG allocation of circa 2.3 million

findings.headline: HRA New Build schemes delivered only £67k of £7.383m budget, with major schemes showing zero expenditure
findings.detail: The council's new build programme slipped by £7.316m (99% of budget). Major schemes including Melish & Sugden (£313k), Innovative Sites (£895k), Mellish Close (£255k), and HRA Levelling Up (£5.919m) each delivered zero expenditure. These are not timing delays but schemes that did not progress at all during the year.
findings.matters: New build delivery is a critical lever for council revenue from future rental streams. Zero expenditure on major schemes indicates either planning/procurement blockage or a change in delivery strategy, either of which would concern a lender about future income generation.
findings.figures: HRA New Build total: £7,383k budget, £67k outturn, £7,316k variance (99% underspend)
findings.quote: Within the residential portfolios a number of major schemes are either transferred or awaiting transfer.

findings.headline: HRA Stock Investment programme facing systemic delivery pressures with £8m reprofiled out of 2026/27
findings.detail: The HRA Stock Investment programme underspent by £7.994m in 2025/26. The narrative explicitly states that historic underspends and staffing resource issues have impacted delivery, and the council is now undertaking a reprofiling exercise to push the underspend into future years rather than carrying it forward into 2026/27. A Head of Capital Delivery and Assets was recently appointed to address this.
findings.matters: Persistent underspend on a major programme signals delivery risk, and the decision to reprofile (not carry forward) suggests the council recognises it cannot deliver this amount in the next year either. This indicates capacity constraints on core housing investment.
findings.figures: HRA Stock Investment underspend: £7,994k; reprofiled underspend: £8,429k
findings.quote: Historic underspends, staffing resource issues have impacted delivery in prior years. Following the appointment of a Head of Capital Delivery and Assets, alongside working with Finance Business Partners a reprofiling into future years exercise is being undertaken as part of the MTFP process, rather than carrying entirety of the 2025/26 underspend into 2026/27.

findings.headline: 71.1% of capital programme financed through borrowing, not other sources
findings.detail: The council's capital funding is heavily dependent on borrowing. Of the £175.7m gross capital spend (including DFC and PFI), £125m came from borrowing while only £50.7m (28.9%) came from grants, CIL, S106, MRR, RCCO and capital receipts. This demonstrates limited internal capacity to fund capital investment from own resources.
findings.matters: A lender would be concerned about a council whose capital programme is dependent on continued borrowing capacity rather than diversified funding sources, and would want to understand the council's medium-term capital strategy.
findings.figures: Borrowing: £124,991k (71.1% of £175,691k total)
findings.quote: The capital programme is financed from various sources, including grant, CIL, S106 contribution, revenue contribution, capital receipts and borrowing.

findings.headline: Leisure contract produced a shortfall requiring £0.240m reserve drawdown
findings.detail: The Budget Support Reserve was drawn down by £0.240m to mitigate a leisure contract shortfall. This suggests the council's leisure services agreement generated an outturn pressure that could not be absorbed within the service budget.
findings.matters: Leisure contracts are often a source of operational pressure; a shortfall in outturn indicates either demand volatility, cost inflation, or contract design issues that affect financial position.
findings.figures: £0.240m drawdown
findings.quote: Draw down to mitigate Leisure Contract Shortfall

findings.headline: Hotel/aparthotel development not meeting income expectations; £0.283m shortfall covered from reserve
findings.detail: The CR27 Hotel Deal reserve was drawn down by £0.283m to cover an Aparthotel rent shortfall, meaning the development is not generating expected rental income. The reserve was opened to manage this risk but is now being drawn.
findings.matters: Capital investment underperformance is a governance concern; if a major council development is not meeting income projections, it raises questions about investment appraisal, market assumptions, and potential for further drawdowns.
findings.figures: £0.283m drawdown
findings.quote: Drawdown from reserve to cover Aparthotel rent shortfall

findings.headline: Children's social care placement costs required £0.535m reserve drawdown
findings.detail: The Children's Social Care Reserve was drawn down by £0.535m to mitigate placement cost pressures. This indicates the council faced outturn pressures in residential and fostering placements, a known area of volatility and cost sensitivity.
findings.matters: Placement cost pressures indicate either higher volumes of children needing care or increased unit costs; both signal underlying service demand that must be managed or funded differently.
findings.figures: £0.535m drawdown
findings.quote: Drawdown from reserve to mitigate placement cost pressures

findings.headline: Schools budget overspent by £6.4m, requiring large reserve drawdown
findings.detail: The council drew £6.416m from the LMS (Local Management of Schools) Reserve to fund schools overspend and capital expenditure in 2025-26. This is the largest single drawdown in the document and indicates significant outturn pressure in the schools budget.
findings.matters: Large schools overspends suggest either deteriorating budget control in a material service or structural funding inadequacy; either is a concern to a lender and the finance director.
findings.figures: £6.416m drawdown from LMS Reserve
findings.quote: Drawdown to fund schools overspend and capital expenditure

findings.headline: Regulatory change from 1 April 2026: Fund must take all strategic investment decisions through London CIV
findings.detail: Under 'Fit for the Future' legislation, the council loses local discretion over pension fund strategy and must use London CIV for all investment advice from April 2026. This centralizes decision-making away from the council and its advisers.
findings.matters: Loss of local control over a major financial asset and the shift to a third-party decision-maker could affect the council's ability to respond quickly to changing circumstances or market conditions.
findings.figures: Effective date: 1 April 2026
findings.quote: From 1 April 2026 under the Fit for the Future legislation the Fund is required to take its strategic investment advice from the London CIV.

findings.headline: Employer contribution rates are reducing and Fund is shifting strategy to generate income to compensate
findings.detail: The paper states that while cashflows have held up, 'the level of employer contribution income will reduce with the reductions in the employer contribution rate.' In response, the Fund is increasing allocation to income-generating assets like UK Gilts and committing to closely monitor impact. This is a specific response to anticipated revenue pressure on the pension fund.
findings.matters: Reducing employer contributions improves the council's near-term budget position, but also signals the Fund must become self-sustaining through investment income, which could constrain future strategic flexibility.
findings.figures: Employer contribution rate reductions not quantified in this paper; Credit allocation increasing from 12% to 17% for growth fixed income
findings.quote: the level of employer contribution income will reduce with the reductions in the employer contribution rate. Fund Officers will closely monitor the impact on the Fund. Asset classes which generate reliable income flows, such as UK Gilts, is an important consideration in the new SAA.

findings.headline: Pension fund's improved funding position enables shift from growth to defensive assets
findings.detail: The triennial valuation (31 March 2025) showed an improved funding position, allowing the Fund to reduce risk exposure by shifting from 53% to 48% in listed equities while increasing UK Government Bonds from 0% to 10%. This defensive repositioning is described as a way to 'lock in the investment gains made' while reducing Value at Risk by 8%.
findings.matters: An improving pension fund position reduces the risk of future calls on the council's general fund budget, which is a material liability for lenders assessing the council's balance sheet sustainability.
findings.figures: Listed Equities reducing from 53% to 48%; UK Government Bonds increasing from 0% to 10%; Value at Risk reduction of 8%; forecast return of 6.5% vs 6.6% for current strategy
findings.quote: The funding position has improved and as a result the Fund can consider reducing its exposure to higher risk asset classes- essentially as a defensive move to lock in the investment gains made.

findings.headline: Minimum Revenue Provision policy tightened: removal of 'stabilisation period' will accelerate revenue charges on IAS assets
findings.detail: The Council is removing its "stabilisation period" for Minimum Revenue Provision on IAS developments. Previously, MRP was deferred for a period after capital expenditure; now it will be charged in the year after assets become operational. This accelerates revenue charge recognition and reduces reported headroom.
findings.matters: The accounting change is a recognition that previous policies masked the true annual cost of IAS debt. As MRP charges accelerate, they will reduce General Fund budget flexibility and increase pressure on Council budgets. It suggests the prior stabilisation approach was not sustainable.
findings.figures: MRP policy change effective 2026/27 for all IAS assets. Specific financial impact not quantified in report but applies to entire IAS portfolio (£1,120m debt).
findings.quote: MRP is to commence in the year after an asset becomes operational or the year after the capital expenditure is incurred (whichever is later)... The 'stabilisation period' in place in MRP policy up to 2025/26 is to be removed
