findings.headline: Essential capital maintenance has been deferred and is now being brought forward under pressure
findings.detail: General Fund capital spending is rising to £63.5m in 2026/27 from £44.2m in 2025/26. The Council states this reflects "essential work which can no longer be held back, such as essential fleet replacement"—signalling that maintenance of core assets was deferred due to capital constraints and IAS investment priorities.
findings.matters: Deferred fleet replacement and maintenance accumulates into cascade failures. It indicates capital rationing was binding, and the Council prioritised debt/investment spending over service delivery infrastructure. As deferred work now comes due, it will pressure budgets further.
findings.figures: General Fund capital: £44.180m (2025/26) → £63.478m (2026/27). Total capital: £196.121m → £126.672m. IAS decline accounts for £104.5m of the total reduction, forcing GF work forward.
findings.quote: There is an increase in the General Fund capital programme reflecting essential work which can no longer be held back, such as essential fleet replacement

findings.headline: Forced into cyclical Local Authority lending with seasonal tightening just when cashflow deteriorates
findings.detail: The Council had "been relying overly heavily on Local Authority borrowing". It took £470m of 12-month PWLB funding in late 2024–early 2025 to diversify, but continues to rely on short-term LA lending because "the availability and associated rates are highly cyclical" and "Council cashflows generally deteriorate in the second half of the year"—precisely when refinancing is hardest.
findings.matters: Seasonal illiquidity in LA lending markets coincides with the Council's weakest cashflow period. If broader credit conditions tighten (recession, systemic stress), the Council's ability to roll short-term debt becomes uncertain just when it is most vulnerable.
findings.figures: £470m of 12-month PWLB funding taken Dec 2024–Mar 2025 in four tranches. Refinancing rates 0.75–1% lower than prior year. Operational reliance on LA lending continues despite diversification attempt.
findings.quote: the Council had been relying overly heavily on Local Authority borrowing- the availability and associated rates are highly cyclical, Council cashflows generally deteriorate in the second half of the year

findings.headline: Interest rates above 5% have made long-term borrowing unaffordable when IAS business cases assumed 3%
findings.detail: The Council's Investment and Acquisitions Strategy was built on interest rate assumptions of 3%. Current PWLB rates range from 4.81% (5-year) to 5.78% (50-year). The Council states that locking in long-term borrowing at these rates is "not manageable" and is instead forced to rely on short-term borrowing, creating refinancing risk. IAS capital expenditure collapsed from £121m in 2025/26 to £17m in 2026/27—an 86% drop.
findings.matters: Residential investment schemes planned to yield 3% become loss-making or unviable at 5% borrowing costs. The Council cannot pursue its investment strategy without locking in unmanageable debt service. If rates stay high, the entire IAS asset base becomes a liability.
findings.figures: IAS business case assumption: 3%. Current PWLB rates: 5-year 4.81%, 10-year 5.39%, 50-year 5.78%. IAS capital expenditure: £121.299m (2025/26) → £16.794m (2026/27).
findings.quote: the IAS business cases typically assumed a rate of 3% and with rates above 5% the adverse financial impact of locking in to long term rates is not manageable

findings.headline: IFRS 16 accounting from April 2024 will bring all new council leases onto the balance sheet, triggering additional MRP charges.
findings.detail: From 1 April 2024, all new leases must be recorded on the council's balance sheet with a matching liability in the Capital Financing Requirement. These will incur MRP charges in the same way as finance leases, which will increase the General Fund's debt repayment obligations.
findings.matters: New lease arrangements from April 2024 onwards will create additional MRP charges that affect General Fund affordability. The council's lease portfolio is not quantified in this document.
findings.figures: Applies from 1 April 2024.
findings.quote: IFRS 16 relating to new arrangements from 1 April 2024 for leases whereby all leases come onto the balance sheet with a matching liability included in the CFR will incur additional MRP charges in the same way as leases previously classified as finance leases.

findings.headline: The council will end its non-compliant MRP policy on IAS residential schemes from April 2026, moving to statutory-guidance-compliant charging.
findings.detail: The council had previously departed from statutory guidance on MRP for IAS residential schemes by not charging MRP until two years after assets became operational. This policy will change from 1 April 2026 to ensure compliance with current regulations. The change will result in MRP being charged under the annuity method over 50 years (40 years for modular properties).
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council was operating outside statutory guidance on a material area, and that from April 2026 the General Fund will incur additional MRP charges on IAS schemes, reducing financial headroom.
findings.figures: MRP period: 50 years for IAS schemes, 40 years for modular/prefabricated properties.
findings.quote: The Council has previously opted to depart from the guidance in relation to the charging of MRP on the IAS residential schemes. On such IAS related expenditure the Council had adopted a policy of not commencing to charge MRP until a period of two years after the asset first became operational. This policy in relation to IAS assets will change from 1 April 2026 to ensure that the Council is compliant with the current Regulations.

findings.headline: Interest costs are budgeted to rise significantly, adding to revenue pressures
findings.detail: The council expects material increases in interest payable and receivable as treasury activity increases. While managers note actual costs are expected to be lower than budgeted, the scale of the budgeted increase indicates debt servicing will consume a larger share of the revenue account.
findings.matters: Rising interest costs reduce capacity to fund services and increase sensitivity to interest rate movements, particularly if the council proceeds with increased borrowing to close the funding gap.
findings.figures: Interest budget increase described as 'significant' with 'large increase in interest payable and receivable'
findings.quote: The interest budget will also change significantly with a large increase in interest payable and receivable.

findings.headline: Significant short-term borrowing requires refinancing; council must either borrow further or sell assets to close the funding gap
findings.detail: The liability benchmark identifies a material short-term borrowing position requiring refinancing. The council acknowledges that bridging the gap between its liabilities and available resources will require borrowing or asset sales. Both options indicate constrained liquidity and limited resources to absorb the capital programme from revenue.
findings.matters: Dependence on asset sales or increased borrowing to fund the capital programme signals potential cash flow stress, reduces financial flexibility, and indicates the council may face difficulties if asset sales do not materialise or if refinancing becomes costlier.
findings.figures: Liability benchmark spans 2025–2094; short-term borrowing and LOBO loans shown as material components in the chart
findings.quote: The liability benchmark shows there is a significant borrowing requirement for both completion of the current capital programme but also to refinance borrowing, including the current significant short-term borrowing position. It is important to note that the borrowing requirement is lower than in past years as the capital programme has reduced. To reduce the gap will require borrowing or the sale of assets and both options are being looked at.

findings.headline: Reserves are being depleted to fund annual shortfalls, forcing increased borrowing as cash diminishes
findings.detail: The council explicitly states it is using reserves to cover shortfalls in its funding. As reserves deplete, this reduces internal borrowing capacity and shrinks cash balances, requiring the council to borrow closer to its Capital Financing Requirement level. This creates a deteriorating cash position where reserves act as a buffer for ongoing structural deficits.
findings.matters: Using reserves to cover annual funding gaps signals the council cannot balance its budget from ongoing revenues, indicating systemic financial stress with limited headroom for adverse developments.
findings.quote: The under borrowed position is likely to reduce over time as the Council's reserves are reduced to fund shortfalls in the Council's funding. The use of reserves will result in a reduction in internal borrowing, which will also reduce the Council's cash balances, requiring the Council to borrow to closer to the CFR level.

findings.headline: A strategic review of all property assets will consider disposals and whether to avoid additional Council borrowing.
findings.detail: Management is preparing a report on a new way of working covering all council property assets, with a focus on increasing income through better management, redevelopment, or disposal. Explicitly frames future strategy as working 'without additional Council borrowing', confirming that affordability constraints are driving asset decisions.
findings.matters: This signals the council is considering asset disposals to reduce debt exposure and fund operations without new borrowing — a defensive move in response to interest rate pressure.
findings.figures: Historic commercial portfolio: 127 properties generating £6.5m per annum
findings.quote: A new Inclusive Growth and Place Strategy in 2026 will set this out within the broader context of still delivering growth and benefits for residents but without additional Council borrowing.

findings.headline: The council holds a £200m commercial property portfolio acquired under the IAS and financed predominantly by borrowing.
findings.detail: As part of the IAS, the council acquired 20 commercial assets worth approximately £200m, mostly funded by debt. These generate £6.85m annual rental income. Given the interest rate environment that has frozen new IAS schemes, this portfolio's underlying returns may no longer justify the borrowing cost.
findings.matters: A large commercial portfolio funded by debt in a rising-rate environment represents ongoing refinancing and valuation risk, particularly if property values or rents weaken.
findings.figures: £200m portfolio value; £6.85m per annum rental income; 20 assets
findings.quote: As part of the IAS the Council has acquired a portfolio of commercial investments, comprising 20 assets with a value of c£200m which currently generate £6.85m per annum rent. The portfolio was predominantly financed by borrowing.

findings.headline: The council has halted new Investment Acquisition Strategy schemes and will only complete pre-planned projects.
findings.detail: High inflation and interest rates have forced a strategic pause. No new IAS schemes will proceed; only existing commitments will complete. This represents a major change in capital strategy and reflects affordability constraints despite the 4,000-unit housing ambition previously announced.
findings.matters: Stopping new IAS schemes signals that interest rates have breached the affordability threshold for growth investment, a material constraint on the council's financial flexibility.
findings.figures: 60 schemes previously; now limited to completions only
findings.quote: High inflation and increased interest rates have had a significant impact on the Council's capital strategy particularly in relation to its Investment Acquisition Strategy (IAS). Schemes already planned have been or will be completed but no new schemes will be undertaken within the IAS.

findings.headline: Interest rate rises are forcing the council to cut interest rates on IAS projects to maintain viability, adversely impacting cash flows back to the council.
findings.detail: The council's £2bn Investment Acquisition Strategy was built on historic 2% borrowing costs. With interest rates now significantly higher, schemes developed by Be First become unviable at market rates. The council is reducing the interest rate charged to subsidiary Reside to keep projects alive, directly reducing the cash flows expected to flow back to fund borrowing repayment.
findings.matters: This creates a structural mismatch between borrowing costs and asset returns, eroding the financial case for the entire IAS programme and leaving the council absorbing the gap.
findings.figures: £2bn capital spend across 60 schemes; 2% average historic PWLB rate vs. current rates significantly above that
findings.quote: The sharp upward trend in interest rates means that new projects need to be charged at a rate significantly above the 2% average for the Council's historic long term PWLB borrowing. The higher borrowing cost may make the developed scheme unviable for Reside so the interest rate charged is therefore reduced to ensure viability for the project. This has an adverse impact on the long term cash flows back from Reside to fund the borrowing costs.

findings.headline: IAS accounting pressure of £3.7m in 2026/27 reflects pension and financial reporting costs
findings.detail: The council faces a £3.7m pressure in 2026/27 related to International Accounting Standard (IAS) requirements, typically relating to pension valuations and other accounting adjustments. This declines to £352k (2027/28) and £1.2m (2028/29), suggesting a one-off revaluation in 2026/27.
findings.matters: While IAS pressures are often non-cash in nature, they reflect balance sheet movements (typically pension liabilities) that indicate the council's longer-term financial obligations.
findings.quote: Pressure Central IAS 3,692 352 1,168

findings.headline: Previously planned waste disposal income savings reverse in 2027/28, costing £1m
findings.detail: The council planned to increase waste disposal income by £1.5m in 2026/27, but this reverses in 2027/28 with a £1m cost, suggesting the planned income increase cannot be sustained. Housing income shows the same pattern: £1.5m increase planned for 2027/28 reverses to a £500k cost in 2028/29.
findings.matters: Savings reversals suggest the council's financial planning assumptions may not be holding up over the planning period. A lender would be concerned about the sustainability of the council's five-year financial plan if major saving assumptions are being reversed within two years.
findings.quote: Savings Housing, Environment & Communities Waste Disposal - Increase Income (1,508) 1,000 508; Savings Housing, Environment & Communities Housing Income (500) (1,500) 500

findings.headline: Central contingency allocation of £2.8m rising to £4m from 2027/28 suggests budget plan uncertainty
findings.detail: The council is allocating £2.8m contingency in 2026/27, then increasing this to £4m in 2027/28 and holding it there through 2029/30. The increase from £2.8m to £4m suggests growing concern about whether planned savings or income can be achieved. This contingency represents unallocated funds held back due to uncertainty.
findings.matters: Contingency allocations indicate the council does not have full confidence in achieving its planned savings or generating expected income. The year-on-year increase suggests deteriorating certainty, which is a risk indicator for financial stability.
findings.figures: Contingency Central Central Contingency/BSR Top-Up: £2,848k (2026/27), £4,000k (2027/28), £4,000k (2028/29)
findings.quote: Contingency Central Central Contingency/BSR Top-Up 2,848 4,000 4,000

findings.headline: Major debt servicing burden of £3.4m in 2026/27 indicates substantial prior borrowing
findings.detail: The council is allocating £3.4m to Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP) in 2026/27, which covers debt repayment and servicing of existing borrowing. While this falls to £854k in 2027/28 and £556k in 2028/29, the initial £3.4m figure indicates substantial prior borrowing decisions or capital programmes that are now requiring servicing.
findings.matters: MRP is a mandatory revenue cost to service existing debt and directly reduces the council's financial flexibility. A lender would need to understand the council's existing debt burden and capacity to service additional borrowing.
findings.quote: Contractual Central MRP 3,402 854 556 400

findings.headline: Adult social care faces structural inflation and demand growth of £10m+ annually
findings.detail: The council faces £4.7m annual inflationary pressure on adult social care, remaining above £3.8m annually through 2030/31, plus £3.3m learning disability demand (growing to £1.3m incremental annually) and £2m homecare demand in 2026/27. These are not one-off costs but recurring structural pressures in the council's largest service.
findings.matters: Adult social care is typically a council's largest budget area and these pressures indicate structural cost growth that cannot be avoided through service reductions. The demand growth in learning disability and homecare suggests increasing caseloads and complexity.
findings.figures: Adults - Inflationary Pressures: £4,708k (2026/27), £4,010k (2027/28), £3,831k (2028/29); Learning Disability Demand: £3,252k (2026/27); Homecare: £2,000k (2026/27)
findings.quote: Demand People and Resilience Homecare 2,000 663 730 788 851; Demand People and Resilience Learning Disability Demand 3,252 764 905 1,090 1,324; Inflation People and Resilience Adults - Inflationary Pressures 4,708 4,010 3,831 4,174 4,174

findings.headline: Reside (housing management subsidiary) experiencing handover and void delays, causing income loss
findings.detail: The council's housing subsidiary Reside is experiencing operational problems. The paper notes 'a number of problems with the handover processes at practical completion and the letting of new properties, particularly the market rent tenure. This has caused a loss of income to the IAS.' For schemes under construction, this delays the point at which income flows can service the underlying debt. This is an execution risk in the subsidiary, not just a financial one.
findings.matters: Void and lettings delays on an indebted housing portfolio create servicing risk. Income shortfalls cascade to the council if the subsidiary cannot meet its loan covenant payments.
findings.figures: IAS income contribution down from £4.7m (2025/26) to £1m (2026/27); void/lettings issue is operational but unquantified
findings.quote: The Council has encountered a number of problems with the handover processes at practical completion and the letting of new properties, particularly the market rent tenure. This has caused a loss of income to the IAS.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant overspend of £3.1m in High Needs Block; driven by SEND demand escalation
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant is forecasting a £3.1m overspend in the High Needs Block (Q3 2025/26), driven by 'growth in alternative resource provision (ARP) and special school places, increased home tuition demand, rising post-16 SEND activity and higher commissioned service costs.' This is a demand that is growing and cannot be cut without statutory risk.
findings.matters: SEND demand is a national issue but represents an uncontrollable cost pressure. School deficits create cumulative debt that the council must eventually absorb into the General Fund.
findings.figures: £3.1m High Needs Block overspend (Q3 2025/26); projected DSG deficit of £1.9m
findings.quote: The DSG forecast overspend has increased marginally from £3.0m at Quarter 2 to £3.1m at Quarter 3, with pressures continuing to fall entirely within the High Needs Block.

findings.headline: £1.9m of approved 2025/26 savings off-track and reliant on management intervention to deliver
findings.detail: As of Q3 2025/26, £1.9m of the council's approved savings programme is categorized as 'off track but expected to be delivered following continued management intervention.' This suggests that identifying and delivering savings is proving difficult and the council is relying on emergency action to meet its targets.
findings.matters: Off-track savings in the current year signal that future savings targets (critical to bridging the MTFS gap) may also be at risk.
findings.figures: £1.9m off-track savings (Q3 2025/26); £16.1m total savings programme for 2025/26
findings.quote: £1.9m is categorised as Off Track but is currently expected to be delivered following continued management intervention.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation demand remains a material uncontrolled risk despite no 2026/27 budget pressure assumed
findings.detail: Although the council is not assuming a budget pressure for temporary accommodation in 2026/27 (due to 'future local housing supply and homelessness accommodation allocation strategy changes'), the paper flags that 'there is still significant risk that demands on Temporary Accommodation could continue to grow and furthermore create cost implications for the council.' Economic uncertainty and London housing shortage suggest this risk is real, and if activated, would create material in-year pressure.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is a volatile, demand-led cost that the council cannot fully control. A downside scenario on housing supply would create budget pressure mid-year.
findings.figures: No 2026/27 budget increase assumed; noted as 'significant risk' with ongoing monitoring required
findings.quote: Due to future local housing supply and homelessness accommodation allocation strategy changes, the council is not facing a core budget pressure in 2026/27 and hence no increase in budget is assumed. However, there is still significant risk that demands on Temporary Accommodation could continue to grow and furthermore create cost implications for the council.

findings.headline: Council Tax base declining — down 620 properties (1.07%) year-on-year
findings.detail: The Council Tax base for 2026/27 has decreased from the prior year by 620 band D equivalent properties, a 1.07% decline. Despite setting council tax at the maximum permissible 4.99%, the council is losing taxable capacity, likely reflecting residents' inability to pay and/or demographic shifts. The paper assumes only 1.8% growth in the tax base for future years.
findings.matters: A shrinking tax base despite a cost of living crisis indicates either population loss or reduced property values, and limits the council's ability to raise revenue locally.
findings.figures: Council Tax Base decline 620 band D equivalent (1.07%); budgeted collection rate 95%
findings.quote: The calculation of the 2026/27 council tax base resulted in the decrease in Council Tax Base by 1.07% (which is 620 band D equivalent properties) when compared to 2025/26.

findings.headline: Withdrawal from business rates pool removes previously budgeted income stream
findings.detail: The council has withdrawn from a tri-borough business rates pool arrangement with Havering and Thurrock because 'the financial benefits previously gained from pooling arrangements are no longer available following the national business rates reset.' This removes an income source the council had previously relied on, though the paper does not quantify the loss. The pool was not included in the Provisional Local Government Settlement.
findings.matters: Loss of previously anticipated pooling income reduces financial flexibility and represents a structural reduction in available funding.
findings.figures: Specific quantified loss not disclosed
findings.quote: The Council has withdrawn from the Business Rates Pool for 2026/27 because the financial benefits previously gained from pooling arrangements are no longer available following the national business rates reset. The reset has significantly reduced the growth retained locally by member authorities, meaning the pool no longer generates a net financial gain for the Council.

findings.headline: Already forecasting £2.8m General Fund overspend in 2025/26, with People & Resilience £7.7m over
findings.detail: Despite being mid-way through 2025/26, the council is already forecasting a £2.8m General Fund overspend (Q3). The People & Resilience directorate is forecasting a £7.7m overspend against a £143m budget (5.4% overspend). This is not a one-off issue: grant-funded contingencies have had to be deployed to manage pressure. The paper notes 'The financial challenges facing P&R in the current financial year are expected to persist, and potentially intensify, over the coming period.'
findings.matters: In-year overspend, even with contingency deployment, signals that base budgets are not matching actual service costs and reserve sustainability is at risk.
findings.figures: £2.8m General Fund overspend forecast (Q3 2025/26); £7.7m People & Resilience overspend (5.4% of directorate budget); £4m corporate contingency deployed
findings.quote: The financial challenges facing P&R in the current financial year are expected to persist, and potentially intensify, over the coming period.

findings.headline: Children's residential placement costs up 46% in one year; volumes also increasing
findings.detail: The council faces severe cost inflation in children's social care. Private residential placement costs have increased 46% in a single year, and the council now has 49 more children in care than the previous year. Q3 2025/26 forecasts a £2.7m overspend in Children's Care & Support driven by 'significant placement cost inflation' and 'higher placement volumes'. This is not a demand-management issue the council controls.
findings.matters: Rapid cost escalation in a statutory service (child protection) with rising caseloads removes budget flexibility and creates uncontrollable cost pressure.
findings.figures: 46% increase in private residential placement costs; +49 children in care vs prior year; £2.7m Q3 2025/26 overspend in Children's Care & Support
findings.quote: Children's Care & Support: A £2.7m pressure resulting from significant placement cost inflation, including a 46% increase in private residential placement costs, higher placement volumes (+49 children in care compared with 2024), and the partial delivery of MTFS savings.

findings.headline: Adult social care market costs escalating with no control; Learning Disability placements reaching £5,000 per week
findings.detail: The council faces rising demand and 'greater complexity of need' in adult social care. The paper reports 'significant changes in the nature of needs within that ASC care' with working-age adults now a larger cohort. High-cost Learning Disability placements are reaching £5,000 per week. Market care providers received a 5% uplift in 2025/26, and the council faces £4.9m pressure in Adults Care in Q3 2025/26 driven by increased demand, cost inflation, and high-cost placements. The council is 'holding a firm line' in negotiations but faces continued upward pressure.
findings.matters: Uncontrollable escalation in social care costs — driven by demographic change and market-driven price inflation — is a core driver of the council's medium-term deficit and represents a commitment the council cannot easily reduce.
findings.figures: £4.9m Adults Care pressure (Q3 2025/26); Learning Disability placements £5k/week; market provider uplift 5% (2025/26); demographic shift to working-age population with higher support needs
findings.quote: LBBD continues to see rises in requests for support and assessments, and significant changes in the nature of needs within that ASC care, from older to working age adults, and complexity of that care has increased over the last five years.

findings.headline: Commercial asset portfolio not performing financially; strategic review underway with external advisors
findings.detail: The council holds a commercial investment portfolio 'predominantly acquired by way of land assembly for regeneration schemes' that 'is currently not performing financially'. A strategic review with external advisors has been commissioned to develop an asset management plan and improve efficiency. This represents a loss-making asset base with no clear recovery path stated in the paper.
findings.matters: An underperforming property portfolio creates potential for further asset write-downs, disposal losses, or continued revenue drag — and suggests the council's IAS subsidiary structure and asset strategy require external remediation.
findings.figures: No quantified loss stated; total borrowing for IAS as at 31 December 2025 was £1.1bn
findings.quote: This portfolio is currently not performing financially, and the Council has commenced a strategic review in conjunction with external advisors and subsidiaries to put in place an asset management plan to improve the efficiency and rationalise the commercial assets.

findings.headline: Investment and Acquisition Strategy unviable — £138m additional borrowing required despite interest rate risk
findings.detail: The council's flagship IAS, intended to be self-financing with a 5% revenue return, is no longer viable. Rising interest rates and construction cost inflation have caused schemes to fail viability tests. The council must borrow an additional £138m to complete existing approved schemes. The paper notes the portfolio is 'currently not performing financially' and a strategic review with external advisors is underway. The IAS income contribution to the General Fund has collapsed from £4.7m (2025/26 forecast) to £1m (2026/27 budget).
findings.matters: £138m of new borrowing for schemes no longer meeting their original financial case represents material debt growth with uncertain income generation, and indicates the council overestimated its development capacity and cost assumptions.
findings.figures: £138m additional borrowing required; IAS income down from £4.7m to £1m year-on-year; total IAS borrowing as at 31 December 2025 was £1.1bn
findings.quote: The rise in interest rates and the high inflation costs within the construction sector have led to a number of schemes costing more than originally planned and new schemes unable to pass the viability assessments. Whilst this has led to a pause on new schemes, there will still be a requirement for the Council to borrow an additional £138m to complete the existing approved schemes.

findings.headline: Council faces cumulative budget deficit of £82.4m by 2030/31 without transformational change to service models
findings.detail: The council has achieved a balanced 2026/27 budget but faces a deficit of £5.7m for 2027/28 that grows cumulatively to £82.4m by the end of the medium-term plan in 2030/31. The paper explicitly states: 'At current service models and cost levels, the Council's financial position will be unsustainable over the MTFP period. Incremental or salami slicing savings will no longer be sufficient to close the gap.'
findings.matters: A five-year structural deficit of this scale, despite a balanced 2026/27 position, indicates fundamental financial unsustainability and severe pressure on debt capacity and service provision.
findings.figures: £5.7m deficit 2027/28; cumulative £82.4m by 2030/31
findings.quote: At current service models and cost levels, the Council's financial position will be unsustainable over the MTFP period. Incremental or 'salami slicing' savings will no longer be sufficient to close the gap.

findings.headline: Regeneration pipeline has £25m costs incurred but scheme viability remains uncertain
findings.detail: The council has incurred approximately £25m in costs on a regeneration pipeline where "scheme viability remains challenging." A partnership model has been approved to reduce the council's reliance on borrowing to deliver these schemes.
findings.matters: Substantial sunk costs on schemes with unresolved viability create risk of further investment or potential write-downs, affecting financial position and future debt capacity.
findings.figures: Approximately £25m in costs already incurred
findings.quote: A number of pipeline regeneration schemes for which approximately £25m in costs have already been incurred, although scheme viability remains challenging.

findings.headline: £1.8m of £8.7m planned savings are Invest-to-Save schemes still only in development, not yet committed
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget includes £8.7m of savings. Of these, £1.8m are Invest-to-Save initiatives which are "currently in development, with delivery subject to oversight and assurance from the Change Board." This means 21% of the savings target remains undelivered.
findings.matters: Undeveloped savings schemes increase the risk that the full savings target will not be met, potentially creating a budget shortfall requiring further corrective action.
findings.figures: £1.8m of £8.7m savings remain Invest-to-Save in development
findings.quote: The Invest‑to‑Save savings are currently in development, with delivery subject to oversight and assurance from the Change Board.

findings.headline: Audit disclaimers on 2023/24 and 2024/25 accounts; full assurance not expected until 2029/30
findings.detail: Previous auditors BDO disclaimed accounts for 2019/20–2022/23. Current auditors Grant Thornton will disclaim 2023/24 and 2024/25 accounts in February 2026. Auditors have indicated it may take a further three years to reach full assurance, meaning the council will have no fully audited accounts until 2029/30.
findings.matters: Multi-year audit disclaimers indicate material internal control weaknesses and delay financial assurance. Lenders require timely audited accounts to assess financial position.
findings.figures: 2019/20–2025/26 accounts disclaimed or projected to be disclaimed; three additional years to full assurance
findings.quote: Grant Thornton, the Councils current external auditors, will conclude the 2023/24 and 2024/25 accounts in February 2026, and these will be disclaimed. The auditors have indicated that it may take a further three years to reach a position where full assurance can be provided.

findings.headline: Council is forecasting a £2.8m overspend in 2025/26 with months remaining in the financial year
findings.detail: At Period 9 (November), the council is tracking to overspend by £2.8m in the current year. Officers are working on mitigations but have not yet resolved the position. If the overspend materialises, reserve balances will be impacted.
findings.matters: An in-year overspend indicates budget control is weaker than anticipated and will erode reserves heading into the budget year, reducing financial headroom.
findings.figures: £2.8m overspend at Period 9 2025/26
findings.quote: It is to be noted at Period 9, the Council is forecasting an overspend of £2.8m for 2026/26.

findings.headline: Investment and Acquisition Strategy income fell 79% year-on-year from £4.7m to £1m target for 2026/27
findings.detail: The IAS was established to be self-financing through income-generating residential and commercial assets. However, the revenue income budget has fallen 79% year-on-year due to increased interest rates, lower operational returns, and scheme delivery problems including voids and delayed completion. The paper states these risks have already materialised in 2025/26.
findings.matters: A core revenue budget assumption underpinning borrowing affordability has deteriorated dramatically, indicating significant portfolio performance issues on the council's major investment vehicle.
findings.quote: In 2025/26 the Council has an income core budget of £4.7m (excluding Hotel income) to be achieved through an overall net return from the IAS. Due to the impacts outlined above, this will be reduced to £1m for the 2026/27 budget

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant overspend of £2.118m driven by £3.3m High Needs Block pressure.
findings.detail: DSG reported an overall overspend of £2.118m, with the High Needs Block overspending by £3.3m. This pressure is partially offset by underspends in other blocks but signals continued demand pressures in school support, particularly for pupils with additional needs.
findings.matters: Growing High Needs pressures are a council-wide challenge; persistent DSG deficits eventually draw on general fund resources if not resolved.
findings.figures: DSG overspend £2.118m; High Needs Block overspend £3.3m
findings.quote: The Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) is reporting an overall overspend of £2.118m. This is driven by an overspend of £3.3m on High needs block but mitigated by underspends in the Schools Central Service block (£1.2m) and the Early years block (£31k).

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account overspend of £6.06m in 2023-24, also taken from HRA reserves.
findings.detail: The HRA outturn showed a £6.06m overspend, drawn from the HRA reserve. This is a significant variance in a housing operation and compounds the general fund pressures.
findings.matters: HRA deficits indicate the council's social housing operation is not self-sustaining and requires subsidy from reserves, reducing financial flexibility and signalling potential challenges in managing the housing stock.
findings.figures: HRA overspend £6.06m
findings.quote: The Housing Revenue Account (HRA) outturn position for 2023/24 showed an overspend of £6.06m. This overspend have been taken out of the HRA reserve.

findings.headline: MTFS projects cumulative budget gaps rising from £8.8m (2024-25) to £17.3m (2026-27) after use of reserves.
findings.detail: The Medium-Term Financial Strategy presented to Assembly shows that after deploying reserves to fund the 2024-25 gap, the council faces unresolved budget shortfalls of £11.7m in 2025-26 and £17.3m in 2026-27. The narrative states the council will "pursue initiatives that will deliver additional income and financial savings to bridge the gap" but no specific measures are detailed in this extract.
findings.matters: Growing unresolved gaps signal that spending and income are structurally misaligned. If savings are not delivered, the council will further deplete reserves or seek to increase borrowing.
findings.quote: The MTFS position as reported to Assembly in February 2024 is summarised below. 2024-25 £8.809m Budget Gap (Cumulative before reserve funding); 2025-26 £11.693m; 2026-27 £17.317m

findings.headline: Usable reserves declined by £17.3m in one year, from £285.36m to £268.03m.
findings.detail: General Fund earmarked reserves specifically fell from £153.99m to £134.60m year-on-year. While the council still holds substantial reserves, the rate of drawdown—driven by operational deficits across general fund, HRA, and DSG—is material. At the current rate the council is consuming reserves to bridge gaps.
findings.matters: Declining reserve buffers limit the council's resilience to unexpected shocks or continued spending pressures, and indicate an unsustainable position if overspends persist.
findings.figures: Total usable reserves 2023-24: £268.027m (down from £285.360m in 2022-23); General Fund earmarked reserves: £134.603m (down from £153.994m)
findings.quote: Balance at 31 March 2024 (268,027) [usable reserves]... Balance at 31 March 2023 (285,360) [usable reserves]

findings.headline: General Fund outturn deficit of £2.626m, representing service-driven overspends drawn from reserves.
findings.detail: The council's final budget for 2023-24 was £194.46m but outturn expenditure reached £197.086m, creating a deficit of £2.626m. The narrative notes this "is the result of inherent service driven overspends across the Council." The deficit was taken directly from General Fund reserves.
findings.matters: Recurring service overspends signal that budgeted service costs are not aligned with actual demand or efficiency, raising questions about financial control and the sustainability of the council's spending plans.
findings.figures: Budget £194.46m, Outturn £197.086m, Deficit £2.626m
findings.quote: The 2023/24 outturn position is £197.086m, resulting in a deficit of £2.626m taken from the General Fund reserves. This is the result of inherent service driven overspends across the Council.

findings.headline: Auditor disclaimed opinion on Pension Fund due to unlawful loans between council and fund totalling £16.9m at year-end.
findings.detail: The external auditor could not obtain sufficient audit evidence to opine on the Pension Fund statements. Predecessor auditors concluded that short-term loans between the Authority and Pension Fund during 2019/20–2022/23 were unlawful. At 31 March 2024, £16.9m of inter-fund lending remained on the balance sheet. The current auditor noted the possible effects could be "both material and pervasive" and therefore issued a disclaimer rather than a qualified opinion.
findings.matters: A material unlawful transaction within the council's pension fund raises governance and compliance concerns that could affect lender confidence and indicate control weaknesses.
findings.figures: £16.9m loan from Pension Fund to Authority at 31 March 2024; £19m loan from Authority to Pension Fund at 1 April 2023
findings.quote: Opening balances at 1 April 2023 include £19 million relating to a loan from the Authority to the Pension Fund recognised in Current Liabilities. Closing balances at 31 March 2024 include £16.9 million relating to a loan from the Pension Fund to the Authority recognised in Current Assets. The predecessor auditor reported these matters as a regulatory concern and concluded that they were unlawful.

findings.headline: Cannot issue audit certificate until predecessor auditors' prior year sign-offs complete and pension fund opinion issued, extending audit uncertainty
findings.detail: Formal audit closure cannot occur until: prior years' audit certificates are issued; pension fund audit opinion is issued; consolidation returns completed; and NAO confirms Whole of Government Accounts work complete. Predecessor auditors' delayed sign-off (17 December 2025) continues to cascade and constrain current audit closure.
findings.matters: Inability to issue audit certificate leaves audit formally open; external stakeholders cannot rely on audit completion; cascading delays from prior years indicate systemic audit capacity or governance issues.
findings.figures: Predecessor auditors signed off 17 December 2025; backstop date 27 February 2026; report date 18 February 2026
findings.quote: we cannot formally conclude the audit and issue an audit certificate in accordance with the requirements of the Local Audit and Accountability Act 2014 and the Code of Audit Practice until the following occurs: the audit certificate for the previous financial years is issued; the audit opinion on the pension fund financial statement is issued

findings.headline: Unable to complete group accounts audit procedures due to missing working papers, preventing verification of subsidiary financial contributions
findings.detail: Council was unable to provide working papers required to support group accounts, preventing full audit procedures on group financial statements.
findings.matters: Inability to audit group entities means council's consolidated financial position cannot be verified; subsidiaries' financial performance and balances unknown; group reserves and liabilities unconfirmed.
findings.figures: Group audit procedures unable to be undertaken; no working papers provided
findings.quote: the Authority was unable to provide the relevant working papers required to support its group accounts. This meant that full audit procedures could not be undertaken on the group financial statements.

findings.headline: Expenditure recognition errors identified in testing with sample amounts ranging from £15,000 to £750,000, but error rate not quantified due to backstop time constraints
findings.detail: Testing identified two instances where management failed to appropriately accrue for or recognise expenditure items above the £10,000 de-minimis threshold. Due to time pressure from the backstop date, extended testing to determine whether errors are isolated or indicative of wider misstatement was not completed.
findings.matters: Unknown error rate in expenditure means financial position may be materially misstated; control weaknesses in accounts payable and accruals processes; reserves and cash position reliability unknown.
findings.figures: Two errors identified; values £15,000 and £750,000; de-minimis threshold £10,000
findings.quote: Our testing identified two instances where management did not appropriately accrue for, or recognise, expenditure items above the de-minimis threshold of £10,000. The values of the affected sample items ranged from £15,000 to £750,000

findings.headline: Income and expenditure testing only 82% complete at cut-off, with 19 of 56 sampled journals unable to be validated due to missing audit evidence
findings.detail: At the report date, 82% of planned income and expenditure testing was complete. Of 56 journals selected for testing, 19 could not be validated because management did not provide sufficient audit evidence. Two significant manual adjustments also lacked sufficient supporting evidence.
findings.matters: 34% failure rate on journal validation indicates poor financial record-keeping and documentation; inability to support significant transactions raises concerns about completeness and accuracy of reported figures; evidence of weak financial controls.
findings.figures: 82% of testing complete; 19 of 56 journals (34%) could not be validated; deadline 16 January 2026, report date 18 February 2026
findings.quote: 19 journals could not be validated because management did not provide sufficient appropriate audit evidence to support the entries by the deadline. Two significant manual adjustments did not have sufficient appropriate audit evidence.

findings.headline: Significant weaknesses in Value for Money arrangements across financial sustainability and governance with seven key recommendations raised
findings.detail: Auditor concluded the Authority has not made proper arrangements for securing economy, efficiency and effectiveness in its use of resources. Significant weaknesses identified in financial sustainability and governance arrangements warrant formal key recommendations.
findings.matters: VFM weaknesses indicate poor resource management and sustainability concerns; signals that financial controls and strategic management are inadequate; impacts credit assessment and service delivery capability.
findings.figures: Seven key recommendations raised; audit capacity constrained by staff continuity issues requiring use of interim staff
findings.quote: we are therefore not satisfied that the Authority has made proper arrangements for securing economy, efficiency and effectiveness in its use of resources, including financial sustainability and governance. As a result, we have raised key recommendations.

findings.headline: IFRS 16 lease accounting materially understates assets by £331m after council failed to recognise major leased properties
findings.detail: Council recognized only £37.25m in right-of-use assets and £258m in lease liabilities under IFRS 16, but failed to record leased properties including Reside leases, CR27 and Travelodge valued at £331m combined. These properties remain misclassified within council dwellings and investment properties. Full contract review to identify all leases remains incomplete, creating ongoing risk of further material misstatement.
findings.matters: Material asset misstatement of £331m affects balance sheet credibility; incomplete lease identification means financial statements may require further significant restatement; undermines financial position assessment for lending decisions.
findings.figures: £331m in leased properties not recognised as ROU assets; £37.25m ROU assets recognised; £258m lease liabilities recognised; £232m of related lease liabilities included while assets excluded
findings.quote: ROU assets are understated by £331m, and the council dwellings and investment property asset categories are overstated by the same amount. Until this work is finalised, there remains a risk that lease arrangements have not been fully identified, which may result in material understatement of both lease liabilities and ROU assets.

findings.headline: Pension Fund loans of £16.9m were found unlawful and non-compliant with regulations, continuing into 2024/25 with no audit assurance
findings.detail: Predecessor auditors concluded that short-term loans between the Authority and Pension Fund did not comply with regulations and were unlawful. These transactions continued into 2024/25 with a closing balance of £16.9m from the Pension Fund to the Authority at 31 March 2024, entirely unsupported by audit evidence.
findings.matters: Unlawful transactions signal serious governance failure and breach of statutory duties; ongoing transactions without corrective action indicate management weakness; pension fund security is at risk.
findings.figures: £16.9 million loan from Pension Fund to Authority at 31 March 2024; transactions continued 2024/25
findings.quote: based on legal advice obtained, there was no evidence that the short-term loans made between the Authority and its Pension Fund during the relevant years complied with the Regulations, and they therefore concluded that these transactions were unlawful.

findings.headline: Audit opinion disclaimed for the fourth consecutive year, with no assurance over opening balances preventing any opinion on financial position
findings.detail: Grant Thornton will issue a disclaimer of audit opinion for 2024/25, following disclaimed opinions from 2019/20 to 2022/23. The absence of audited opening balances fundamentally constrains ability to form any opinion on the council's overall financial position, reserves strategy, and movements in reserves.
findings.matters: A lender cannot assess credit risk without audited financial statements; the finance director has no independent verification of reserves or financial position; four years of unaudited accounts is a critical control failure.
findings.figures: Disclaimed opinions: 2019/20, 2020/21, 2021/22, 2022/23, anticipated 2024/25
findings.quote: The absence of assurance over opening balances fundamentally constrains the ability to issue an unqualified opinion for 2024/25. Where reserves and other balances have not been fully audited, it is not possible to conclude on the overall financial position, reserves strategy and movements in reserves, even where in-year transactions have been subject to audit.

findings.headline: Council is reducing interest rates charged to Reside below market cost to keep regeneration schemes viable, creating adverse revenue impact
findings.detail: Because elevated interest rates make schemes unviable at market borrowing costs, the council has reduced the interest rates charged to Reside (the company delivering schemes) to ensure project viability. This reduces "long term cash flows back from Reside to fund the borrowing costs," transferring the cost of rate support to the council's revenue budget. The specific revenue impact is material but detailed in a separate Cabinet budget report.
findings.matters: Direct impact on council revenue budget to subsidize regeneration company; affects council's underlying financial sustainability and debt service capacity; combined with commercial property portfolio pressure creates multiple revenue headwinds
findings.figures: No specific figures in this document; council acknowledges it can "delay long term borrowing until the interest rates come down" but that approach has "adverse impact on the long term cash flows"
findings.quote: The higher borrowing cost may make the developed scheme unviable for Reside so the interest rate charged is therefore reduced to ensure viability for the project. This has an adverse impact on the long term cash flows back from Reside to fund the borrowing costs.

findings.headline: Council holds £200m commercial property portfolio financed primarily by borrowing, with three hotel investments
findings.detail: As part of the IAS, the council acquired 20 commercial assets worth approximately £200m generating £6.85m annual rental income (3.4% gross yield), funded largely by borrowing. The portfolio additionally includes three hotel investments with no performance detail provided. A separate portfolio of 127 historic commercial properties generates £6.5m annually. Asset management is being consolidated within the council.
findings.matters: Material leveraged position in commercial real estate, especially in cyclical hotel sector; low yield provides limited headroom for rental underperformance or asset value declines; concurrent revenue pressures from other schemes (see theme 3) increase risk if property income falters
findings.figures: £200m commercial portfolio, 20 assets, £6.85m annual rental income, 3 hotel investments, historic portfolio 127 assets generating £6.5m
findings.quote: the Council has acquired a portfolio of commercial investments, comprising 20 assets with a value of c£200m which currently generate £6.85m per annum rent. The portfolio was predominantly financed by borrowing. Additionally the Council acquired interests in three hotel investments.

findings.headline: No new Investment and Acquisition Strategy schemes will be undertaken due to elevated interest rates making financing unviable
findings.detail: The council has suspended new IAS schemes because rising interest rates have increased borrowing costs to levels significantly above the 2% historic average, making schemes unviable for Reside (the development company). Existing schemes will continue, but no new schemes will start. IAS borrowing has contracted from £121.3m to £16.8m year-on-year as a result, constraining the council's £2bn regeneration programme aimed at building 4,000 housing units.
findings.matters: Shows financial strain on the council's core regeneration strategy; constrains future housing supply and revenue from new developments; indicates rising debt service costs are constraining capital ambitions
findings.figures: IAS gross capital expenditure £121.3m (2025/26) to £16.8m (2026/27); historic PWLB borrowing cost average 2% versus new rates significantly above this
findings.quote: High inflation and increased interest rates have had a significant impact on the Council's capital strategy particularly in relation to its Investment Acquisition Strategy (IAS). Schemes already planned have been or will be completed but no new schemes will be undertaken within the IAS.

findings.headline: Capital programme has been reduced, lowering capital financing requirement
findings.detail: The CFR decline across the forecast period is driven by a reduction in the capital programme rather than accelerated debt repayment. General Fund capital expenditure projections show net negative changes each year: £166,663k (2026/27), £18,430k (2027/28), and £34,822k (2028/29).
findings.matters: A reduced capital investment programme may signal financial constraint or indicate the council is deferring infrastructure investment, affecting service delivery capacity and borrowing trajectory.
findings.quote: It is important to note that the borrowing requirement is lower than in past years as the capital programme has reduced.

findings.headline: Significant short-term borrowing position requires refinancing
findings.detail: The liability benchmark analysis identifies a significant amount of short-term borrowing with less than one year maturity that will need to be refinanced. This exposure is shown in the liability benchmark projection and includes temporary borrowing.
findings.matters: Short-term borrowing refinancing exposes the council to interest rate and market access risk; adverse conditions could make refinancing expensive or difficult and increase debt service costs.
findings.figures: Specific quantum of short-term borrowing not quantified; £50m liquidity allowance included in liability benchmark projections
findings.quote: The liability benchmark shows there is a significant borrowing requirement for both completion of the current capital programme but also to refinance borrowing, including the current significant short-term borrowing position.

findings.headline: Council is using reserve drawdowns to fund operational shortfalls, forcing future external borrowing
findings.detail: The council's under-borrowed position is expected to reduce as reserves are depleted to cover funding gaps. This will reduce internal borrowing and cash balances, requiring the council to increase external borrowing toward its Capital Financing Requirement level.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion to cover structural shortfalls indicates underlying liquidity pressure and signals the council will need to access borrowing markets at higher levels, increasing debt service costs.
findings.figures: CFR projected at £1,997,179k (2026/27) declining to £1,944,177k (2028/29); reserve depletion magnitude not quantified
findings.quote: The under borrowed position is likely to reduce over time as the Council's reserves are reduced to fund shortfalls in the Council's funding. The use of reserves will result in a reduction in internal borrowing, which will also reduce the Council's cash balances, requiring the Council to borrow to closer to the CFR level.

findings.headline: General Fund capital programme increasing due to essential work that can no longer be deferred (fleet replacement, etc.)
findings.detail: The council has increased General Fund capital expenditure from previously held levels. It explicitly states that essential work which can 'no longer be held back' (such as essential fleet replacement) is now being progressed. This creates new borrowing pressure on top of existing IAS debt.
findings.matters: Additional capital spending will require additional borrowing or revenue resources at a time when the council is already managing high debt levels and refinancing stress. This constrains budget flexibility.
findings.figures: General Fund capital expenditure £63.5m in 2026/27 vs £44.2m in 2025/26 estimate
findings.quote: There is an increase in the General Fund capital programme reflecting essential work which can no longer be held back, such as essential fleet replacement

findings.headline: Council maintains very limited cash balances and monitors liquidity daily
findings.detail: The council's treasury position includes minimal cash reserves. It holds only £49.1m in bank/money market funds (2025 year-end) against £1,595m total debt. This requires daily cashflow monitoring and leaves little buffer for unexpected pressures or market disruption.
findings.matters: Very tight liquidity limits flexibility in responding to market shocks and increases reliance on market access for day-to-day operations. The council cannot weather funding stress without accessing new short-term borrowing.
findings.figures: £49.1m banks/MMF vs £1,595.3m total external debt (31 December 2025); daily cashflow monitoring
findings.quote: Due to the very limited cash funds held by the Council there is very limited scope for anything other than short term deposits which guarantee security, liquidity but produce limited returns

findings.headline: Removal of MRP 'stabilisation period' means council starts charging debt repayment earlier for IAS projects
findings.detail: The council is removing the stabilisation period from its Minimum Revenue Provision policy. Previously, MRP on IAS projects was deferred; now MRP must commence in the year after an asset becomes operational, or the year after capital expenditure is incurred (whichever is later). This is a material change to when the General Fund begins bearing the cost of IAS debt repayment.
findings.matters: The timing of when MRP charges begin directly affects the General Fund's revenue budget burden. Earlier MRP charges increase the annual revenue cost of the IAS programme and reduce budget headroom for other services.
findings.figures: MRP policy change effective 2026/27; applies to all capital expenditure funded from borrowing
findings.quote: MRP is to commence in the year after an asset becomes operational or the year after the capital expenditure is incurred (whichever is later) for all assets including developments constructed under the Investment and Acquisitions Strategy (IAS). The 'stabilisation period' in place in MRP policy up to 2025/26 is to be removed

findings.headline: Council continues short-term borrowing strategy as long-term rates are unaffordable; £470m PWLB 12-month funding coming due
findings.detail: The council took £470m of 12-month PWLB funding in four tranches from December 2024 to March 2025 to avoid locking into high long-term rates. Refinancing of this has already commenced (with improved rates of 0.75–1% lower than a year ago, but still above 4.5%). The council intends to continue relying on short-term Local Authority and short-term PWLB borrowing, openly stating this 'is not ideal'.
findings.matters: Reliance on rolling short-term borrowing creates liquidity risk if the short-term funding market tightens or council credit rating deteriorates. It also means the council remains exposed to any further interest rate rises during refinancing windows.
findings.figures: £470m of 12-month PWLB funding refinancing in progress; council indicates continuing strategy of short-term borrowing
findings.quote: Given the continuing high level of long term PWLB borrowing the Council will continue to borrow short term from other Local Authorities and the PWLB. This is not ideal

findings.headline: IAS business cases assumed 3% interest rates; current PWLB rates above 5% make long-term borrowing unaffordable
findings.detail: The council's Investment and Acquisitions Strategy (IAS) projects were modelled at 3% interest rates when rates are currently above 5%. This creates an impossible refinancing choice: locking in high long-term rates breaks the project economics, but continuing to rely on short-term borrowing creates perpetual refinancing pressure. The council explicitly states it cannot manage the adverse financial impact of locking into current long-term rates.
findings.matters: The viability of the council's £1,120m IAS debt portfolio depends entirely on interest rate movements it cannot control. If rates stay high or rise further, the council faces either mounting losses on the IAS portfolio or forced asset disposals.
findings.figures: £1,120m of the council's £1,595m total debt (2025 year-end); IAS assumed rate 3%, current PWLB rates 4.81–6.01%
findings.quote: the IAS business cases typically assumed a rate of 3% and with rates above 5% the adverse financial impact of locking in to long term rates is not manageable

findings.headline: Infrastructure allocation increase from 6% to 10% remains unimplemented
findings.detail: A previous strategic decision to increase infrastructure allocation from 6% to 10% has not been executed. The paper notes this as one of the issues requiring attention in the updated Strategic Asset Allocation work, but provides no explanation for the delay or timeline for implementation.
findings.matters: Strategic investment decisions that remain unimplemented raise questions about governance capacity or strategic commitment; a finance director needs to understand why a deliberate policy decision has not been acted on.
findings.quote: The additional investment in Infrastructure to move the allocation from 6% to 10% has not been implemented

findings.headline: Identified risks on procurement execution including delays, cost escalation, and contractor performance
findings.detail: Risk register flags three material risks: procurement delays impacting mobilisation, poor contractor delivery or non-compliance with standards, and budget exceeds due to market volatility. Mitigations include performance-based payment mechanisms, break clauses, quality assurance protocols, and quarterly budget monitoring, but these are mitigation, not prevention, of execution risk.
findings.matters: Delivery of a 4-year £8.5m-£12m capital programme is dependent on procurement execution. Wide cost range (£8.5m-£12m) indicates cost uncertainty. Delays to procurement could affect both timeline and ultimate outturn.
findings.figures: Expected savings £640k-£1.35m if hybrid model delivers; 10% year-on-year efficiency improvement targets
findings.quote: Delay in formal procurement could impact mobilisation timelines and resident safety outcomes. Risk of exceeding budget due to market volatility or scope changes.

findings.headline: Capital investment is reprofiled from existing HRA budgets, not new borrowing
findings.detail: The £8.5m-£12m programme is funded from existing HRA capital allocations: £7.597m already allocated for fire door replacement over four years, combined with Fire Safety Works budget (£3.526m) and Compliance budget (£3.4m). The report explicitly states this is not additional to existing budget—the allocation will be reprofiled once delivery timing is confirmed.
findings.matters: Demonstrates capital discipline and planning discipline. Council is managing a material capital commitment within budgeted parameters rather than requiring emergency borrowing or reserve drawdown.
findings.figures: Existing fire-related HRA budgets total £14.523m over four years; HRA capital budget 2025/26 is £35.701m
findings.quote: The allocation of funding for Fire Doors requested by this report is not additional to the existing HRA capital budget.

findings.headline: Statutory compliance obligation requiring £8.5m-£12m capital investment, with procurement not yet commenced
findings.detail: The council has identified 2,170 fire safety actions across its social housing portfolio that must be addressed to meet Building Safety Act 2022 requirements. Cabinet approval is sought for capital investment reprofiled over four years, structured as a hybrid procurement model (Year 1 standalone contract plus Years 2-4 framework agreement). However, the formal procurement process has not yet started at the time of this Cabinet decision.
findings.matters: Material capital commitment on a non-discretionary statutory obligation. Execution risk exists on a complex procurement model that has not yet commenced, which could impact timeline and cost delivery.
findings.figures: £8.5m-£12m total over four years; £2.1m-£3.0m Year 1; £6.4m-£9.0m Years 2-4; 2,170 actions to be completed
findings.quote: This report seeks Cabinet approval for a capital investment of £8.5m to £12m over four years to deliver a comprehensive fire door and associated works programme across the Council's social housing stock. The programme will address 2,170 outstanding fire safety remedial actions identified through Fire Risk Assessments, ensuring full compliance with statutory fire safety regulations and the Building Safety Act 2022.

findings.headline: BDMS contract costs not embedded in 2024/25 budget despite May 2024 Cabinet approval, resulting in £0.788m overspend on repairs
findings.detail: The council approved the BDMS contract extension with outlined costs (including £1.9m fleet charges) in May 2024, but these figures were not incorporated into the budget set in January 2024, resulting in a £0.788m repairs overspend. This suggests coordination weakness between procurement and budget planning.
findings.matters: A known, approved contract's costs not being embedded in the budget process suggests gaps in budget governance coordination that could lead to recurrent variances and planning failures
findings.figures: £0.788m overspend on Repairs & Maintenance, BDMS fleet costs £1.9m
findings.quote: While the May 2024 Cabinet report on the BDMS contract extension outlined the total contract costs, including the estimated variable fleet charges of £1.9m, these figures were not fully embedded in the 2024/25 budget.

findings.headline: Universal Credit migration expected to create material income pressure in 2025/26 despite strong current rent collection at 101.28%
findings.detail: Although rent collection performance is currently strong (101.28% vs 100.34% target) and Bad Debt Provision was underspent by £2.249m due to UC impact being slower than expected, the council explicitly flags that UC transition impact is expected to intensify in 2025/26 and requires ongoing monitoring.
findings.matters: A material, identified income risk emerging in the next year could reverse recent collection improvements and increase rent arrears, affecting both HRA cash flow and the appropriateness of bad debt provision levels
findings.figures: 2024/25 rent collection 101.28% vs 100.34% target, Bad Debt Provision underspent £2.249m
findings.quote: While current performance is strong, the potential impact of UC migration is expected to be more pronounced in 2025/26 and will require ongoing monitoring.

findings.headline: Water charges rising 34.29% and sewerage 13.58%, requiring £2.82m budget increase in utility costs
findings.detail: The council's utility supplier has notified of significant cost increases effective 2025/26: sewerage charges up 34.29% and water charges up 13.58%. The council proposes increasing the water cost budget by £2.82m and recovering the full cost uplift through leaseholder service charges.
findings.matters: Material utility cost inflation creates budget pressure on operating expenses and requires cost recovery through rents or service charges, which may impact resident affordability and rent collection rates
findings.figures: Sewerage charges +34.29%, water charges +13.58%, water budget increase £2.82m in 2025/26
findings.quote: The Council's supplier for sewerage and water services has advised that charges will rise by 34.29% and 13.58% respectively.

findings.headline: Stock investment needs identified by condition survey are unaffordable within the Business Plan financial parameters, with £8.793m capital slippage in 2024/25
findings.detail: The stock condition survey identified investment requirements that exceed what the HRA can afford under its financial plan. The council experienced £8.793m capital slippage on planned stock investment in 2024/25. The 2024/25 underspend of £6.94m is being redirected to partially address the backlog, but full stock investment needs remain unaffordable.
findings.matters: Deferred maintenance on an aging housing stock creates accumulating repair liability and future cost risk, relevant to both the council's long-term financial sustainability and housing quality obligations to residents
findings.figures: £8.793m capital slippage on HRA stock investment 2024/25, £6.94m additional capital investment funded from 2024/25 underspend
findings.quote: the full investment need identified through the survey was assessed as unaffordable within the financial parameters of the Plan

findings.headline: HRA projected to fall into deficit in year 18 of the 30-year Business Plan, constraining medium-term stock investment capacity
findings.detail: Despite current reserves of £25.614m (above the 10% minimum threshold), the HRA Business Plan models a structural deficit arriving in year 18. The council explicitly states this viability concern is limiting flexibility for additional stock investment even beyond the short term, restricting the use of available underspends.
findings.matters: A projected structural deficit in a ring-fenced housing account signals that current rent and cost assumptions are not sustainable across the 30-year plan horizon, raising questions about the council's long-term housing provision viability and the risk of future rent pressures or service reductions
findings.figures: £25.614m current reserves, year 18 projected deficit in 30-year Business Plan, minimum threshold £12.8m
findings.quote: viability concerns remain over the medium term, as the HRA is projected to fall into deficit in year 18 of the Business Plan. This limits flexibility for further stock investment beyond the short term.

findings.headline: Operational improvements are not translating into resident confidence; perception-performance gap signals potential control or credibility issues
findings.detail: The council acknowledges a 'gap between operational improvements and perceptions': internally, ASB case management, estate investment, and safety work have all improved, yet TP12 (ASB handling) remained flat at 38% year-on-year despite this work. The council states the issue is 'perception not yet catching up with internal process improvements' and calls for 'clearer communication, quicker enforcement, and more visible local action.' This pattern recurs across several measures—the council claims effort but residents do not perceive it, suggesting either delivery is slower than claimed or residents lack visibility into action taken.
findings.matters: A persistent perception-performance gap after investments suggests challenges in execution, communication, or transparency that may indicate wider management control or credibility issues.
findings.figures: TP12 flat at 38% year-on-year (2023/24: 38.3%, 2024/25: 38%); no change despite claimed internal process improvements
findings.quote: While ASB handling has improved internally, TP12 remains flat at 38% which is 20 points below the national benchmark. This gap suggests a need for us to be clearer in the way we communicate with residents about the actions we have taken after they share their concerns with us.

findings.headline: Regulator's powers have expanded and council remains in lower performance tier, raising compliance risk
findings.detail: The 2023 Act removed the previous 'serious detriment' test, meaning the Regulator of Social Housing 'will now be able to carry out integrated and active regulation across all the Regulated Standards' with 'very substantial powers of enforcement available.' Barking and Dagenham has moved from fourth to third quartile among London authorities but still carries large gaps: TP12 (ASB handling) at 38% vs 58% benchmark (−20 points), TP07 (being kept informed) at 44% vs 67% (−23 points), TP11 (neighbourhood contribution) at 41% vs 63% (−22 points). The council itself identifies 'failure to demonstrate progress may result in regulatory scrutiny.'
findings.matters: The regulatory threshold is now lower and the framework more interventionist; a council in third quartile with 20+ point gaps across key measures is at material risk of formal conditions or intervention if momentum slows.
findings.figures: TP07: 44% vs 67% benchmark (−23 pts); TP12: 38% vs 58% benchmark (−20 pts); TP11: 41% vs 63% benchmark (−22 pts)
findings.quote: The 2023 Act removed the previous 'serious detriment' test, which placed a high threshold on the Regulators ability to use powers if they identified a breach of the Consumer Standards. This means where there is evidence about potential landlord failures in the consumer standards then the Regulator will have the same powers as with safety standards.

findings.headline: HRA facing unfunded mandates: compliance costs acknowledged but larger service improvement costs not yet costed or funded
findings.detail: The council states that introduction of TSMs 'has increased the administrative burden and cost to the HRA of complying with the new measures.' More critically, it acknowledges that 'the improvements required, including repairs and complaint resolution, enhanced communication with residents and the need to modernised core services will have a financial impact on the HRA.' While 2025/26 compliance costs were included in the approved budget, larger improvement costs are still being determined and will be 'factored into the next HRA Business Plan over 30 years, following a more detailed proposal of the changes required.' The council explicitly warns: 'Without investment, we risk plateauing and losing the momentum we have worked hard to build.'
findings.matters: Unquantified investment needs in the HRA, combined with a 30-year payback horizon and reliance on future Cabinet approvals for funding, suggests potential pressure on reserves or future borrowing needs.
findings.figures: 2025/26 compliance costs included in approved HRA budget; additional improvement costs to be determined and factored into 30-year Business Plan
findings.quote: The improvements required, including repairs and complaint resolution, enhanced communication with residents and the need to modernised core services will have a financial impact on the HRA. The long-term nature and costs of improving the service to residents will be factored into the next HRA Business Plan over 30 years.

findings.headline: Only one supplier completed the dialogue phase; three of four shortlisted bidders withdrew
findings.detail: Six suppliers initially responded, four were shortlisted for dialogue phase, but only Capita (the incumbent supplier) completed the process and submitted a final tender. Two bidders withdrew before dialogue began and another withdrew after the first week. This single-bidder outcome means there was no competitive pressure on pricing or contract terms.
findings.matters: Single-bidder procurement outcomes weaken value-for-money assurance and competitive pricing on public spending commitments, particularly concerning when the sole bidder is the incumbent supplier.
findings.figures: 6 suppliers submitted Selection Questionnaires; 4 shortlisted for dialogue; 1 completed tender submission
findings.quote: Of the four shortlisted suppliers, two withdrew before dialogue began, and another withdrew after the first week. Only Capita Business Services Ltd completed the dialogue and submitted a final tender.

findings.headline: Contract award proceeded without prior formal governance approval and in breach of Contract Rules
findings.detail: The procurement was led by Ealing as a central purchasing body, but the council's Cabinet did not approve the procurement strategy in advance. The Legal section explicitly notes the arrangement did not follow the council's standard tendering process and was never approved through formal governance channels. Legal states this 'could have come at substantial risk to the Council' and represents 'a lack of understanding of Contract Rules by the awarding department.'
findings.matters: Governance and control weaknesses, including retrospective approval of large contracts and breach of procurement rules, are material audit risks that affect lending decisions and credit assessments.
findings.figures: Contract value £1,442,587 (inc VAT); total value over potential 7-year term including extensions
findings.quote: The retrospective nature of the award means that Contract Rules have not been followed, and this could have come at substantial risk to the Council. This shows a lack of understanding of Contract Rules by the awarding department and the importance of compliance and good governance.

findings.headline: The council is carrying £1bn of IAS borrowing at short-term rates because longer-term rates are unaffordable, increasing refinance risk over the next 12 months
findings.detail: The council notes "a situation where the Council's short-term borrowing position has increased significantly. This is because longer-term rates have been higher than short-term rates making it unaffordable to lock into more certain rates." A significant amount of borrowing must be refinanced in the next 12 months, "likely to be at higher interest rates," and the Treasury Strategy will seek to manage this within prudential indicators but "will result in additional costs."
